\begin{abstract}
A quantum impurity model describes a small interacting subsystem embedded into a large bath of free fermions.
Here we study the computational complexity of  calculating  the ground energy,  thermal equilibrium, and dynamical properties of these models.
Our work reveals a sharp contrast: equilibrium properties can be efficiently approximated by classical means, whereas time evolution can implement a universal quantum computation.
More precisely, let $H$ be the Hamiltonian of an impurity model with $n$ fermionic modes and a constant-size impurity. We show that:
\begin{itemize}
\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}
\item the ground energy of $H$ can be approximated to additive error $\varepsilon$ by a classical algorithm with runtime $\poly(n,1/\varepsilon)$, improving on the quasi-polynomial runtime of the best previously known algorithm;
\item at inverse temperature $\beta$, the Helmholtz free energy and a classical description of the thermofield double state can be computed to precision $\varepsilon$ in time $\poly(n,\beta,1/\varepsilon)$;
\item simulating the time evolution $e^{-iHt}$ is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete, for $H$ that is time-independent and has a fixed, constant impurity size. 
\end{itemize}
Our algorithms exploit exponential suppression of multi-particle  bath excitations in a basis organized by energy scale and Krylov depth. 
Our universality construction realizes a stationary quantum processor whose program arrives in a stream of freely propagating fermions.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Quantum impurity models provide a natural arena for studying the computational cost of interactions in fermionic Hamiltonians. 
The model consists of a small interacting subsystem, called the impurity, embedded in a large bath of free fermions. 
Without the impurity, ground energies, thermal properties, and 
time evolution of free fermions can be efficiently simulated classically~\cite{terhal2002classical}. With interactions spread throughout the system, ground energy estimation can be $\mathsf{QMA}$-complete, even for variants of the Fermi--Hubbard model and electronic-structure Hamiltonians~\cite{schuch2009computational,ogorman2022electronic}. Impurity models interpolate between these two extreme limits. They restrict 
the support of interactions to a small subsystem of size $m$, which is much smaller than the total system size $n$.
However, the interaction can be arbitrarily strong, so it  
can drastically change properties of the system  and its effect can spread throughout the bath.

Originally introduced to describe magnetic impurities in metals~\cite{anderson1961localized}, these models 
now serve as building blocks for material simulations based on 
the dynamical mean-field theory~\cite{georges1996dynamical,kotliar2006electronic}.  The latter approximates an interacting lattice model by an impurity coupled to a self-consistently determined bath.
The resulting calculation repeatedly calls an impurity solver, typically to evaluate
Green's function describing the propagation of an added or removed fermion. Bauer \emph{et al.}\ proposed delegating  this step to a quantum computer while performing  the surrounding self-consistency loop
classically~\cite{bauer2016hybrid}. This raises a basic question: which properties of  impurity models can be computed efficiently by classical algorithms, and where might a quantum computer offer an advantage?

Classical impurity solvers have achieved considerable success. Numerical renormalization group~\cite{wilson1975renormalization,bulla2008numerical,merker2012numerical}, Monte Carlo methods~\cite{gull2011continuous}, and density matrix renormalization group~\cite{white1992density} provide powerful methods for equilibrium calculations. Modern tensor-network solvers, including fork tensor-product states and methods using Gaussian changes of basis, also access spectral functions and real-time response~\cite{wolf2015imaginary,bauernfeind2017fork,wu2025disentangling}. Long-time evolution is often more demanding
because entanglement growth makes compact tensor-network representations increasingly costly to maintain~\cite{grundner2024complex}.
These observations suggest  a distinction between the cost of equilibrium and dynamical simulations for impurity models, which is the main topic
investigated in the present work.

Bravyi and Gosset~\cite{bravyi2017complexity} gave the first classical algorithm for approximating the ground energy of impurity models with rigorous performance guarantees.
Assuming that the impurity size is a fixed constant, the algorithm of~\cite{bravyi2017complexity} 
approximates the ground energy with an additive error $\varepsilon$ in time  polynomial in  the total system size $n$ and exponential in $\log^3{(1/\varepsilon)}$,
that is, quasi-polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$.
Their analysis also established low-rank Gaussian approximations to low-energy states, motivating practical variational algorithms~\cite{boutin2021quantum,snyman2021efficient} and subsequent work on quantum embedding~\cite{erakovic2025high}. In this work, we will be concerned with two central questions, that were posed in the work of~\cite{bravyi2017complexity}: 
\begin{quote}
    \begin{center}
        \emph{\textbf{1.} Is there a  $\poly(n,1/\varepsilon)$-time classical algorithm for the ground energy problem?}\\[1.5mm]
\emph{\textbf{2.} Can a time-independent Hamiltonian with a constant-sized impurity be universal?}
    \end{center}
\end{quote}
Here universality means that time evolution under the considered class of Hamiltonians can realize an arbitrary quantum computation with at most polynomial slowdown; previously, it was known for time-dependent impurity Hamiltonians~\cite{brod2014computational} and for time-independent models whose impurity size grows with $n$~\cite{pham2026time}.

The main contribution of this work is in answering both questions above in the affirmative. Additionally, we  give polynomial-time classical algorithms for computing a number of thermal equilibrium properties, that could be of independent interest.

\subsection{Main results}
\label{sec:main-results}

\paragraph{Model.}
Consider $n$ fermionic modes with annihilation and creation operators
$a_j$ and $a_j^\dagger$, and a small subset
$\mathcal I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ constituting
the impurity.
Each mode can be either empty or occupied by a fermion.
The corresponding $2^n$-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal F_n$, known as the Fock
space, is equipped with the occupation number basis
$\ket{x}$, where $x\in \{0,1\}^n$.
The standard number-conserving impurity Hamiltonian is
\[
H=H_0+V,\qquad
H_0=\sum_{j,k=1}^n h_{jk}a_j^\dagger a_k,\qquad
V=\sum_{j,k,\ell,r\in\mathcal I}
v_{jk\ell r}a_j^\dagger a_k^\dagger a_\ell a_r.
\]
Here $h=h^\dagger$ and the interaction coefficients are chosen so that
$V$ is Hermitian.
The quadratic term $H_0$ describes noninteracting fermions on all $n$
modes, including hopping between the 
impurity and the remaining modes.  
We shall refer to $H_0$ as the \emph{bath Hamiltonian} and choose the energy scale such that $\|h\|=O(1)$.
The quartic term $V$ is the \emph{interaction}: it acts only on the
modes in $\mathcal I$ and may have arbitrary strength.
Following the convention of~\cite{bravyi2017complexity}, let us say that the impurity has size $m=2|\mathcal I|$.
Our results also allow pairing terms in $H_0$ and more general
impurity interactions\footnote{The impurity size $m$ counts the number of Majorana modes in $\mathcal I$.}, as defined precisely in
Section~\ref{sec:impurity-model}.

To describe our results, let us first recall some standard terminology pertaining to fermionic systems, see e.g.~\cite{terhal2002classical,bravyi2004lagrangian,bravyi2017complexity}.
 A {\em Bogoliubov transformation} is a unitary operator
$U$ on the Fock space ${\mathcal F}_n$ such that the conjugated action $a_i \mapsto U^\dagger a_i U$ sends each annihilation operator to a linear combination
of annihilation and creation operators $a_j,a_j^\dagger$ with $j=1,\ldots,n$. Such a unitary $U$ can be succinctly described
by $O(n^2)$ coefficients describing its conjugated action on the annihilation operators.  A fermionic  {\em Gaussian state} is a state of the form $U|x\rangle$, where
$U$ is a Bogoliubov transformation and $x\in \{0,1\}^n$ is a Fock basis vector 
(here we only consider pure Gaussian states).

\paragraph{Ground state estimation.} 
Our first computational task is to approximate the global ground
energy of the Hamiltonian $H$, i.e., approximate the quantity
\[
    E_1(H)
    :=
    \min_{\substack{\phi\in\mathcal F_n\\
                    \lVert\phi\rVert=1}}
    \langle\phi|H|\phi\rangle,
\]
up to accuracy $\varepsilon \in (0,1/2)$ and given an input of the compact classical description of \(H\).

Our first result gives both an approximation to the ground energy and
a succinct classical description of a state attaining approximately
that energy.
\begin{theorem}[Ground-energy approximation]
\label{thm:ground-energy-algorithm}
\label{thm:main}
Let $\varepsilon \in (0,1/2)$. Let $H=H_0+V$ be a Hamiltonian describing a quantum impurity model with $n$ fermionic modes and impurity size $m$ with $1\le m\le n$. Let $E_1(H)$ be the smallest eigenvalue of $H$. There is a classical algorithm that computes $\widehat{E}_1$ satisfying
$$
E_1(H) \leq \widehat{E}_1 \leq E_1(H)+\varepsilon.
$$
The algorithm has runtime $\poly(n,1+\|V\|)\, \exp[O(m\log(m/\varepsilon))]$.
The algorithm also computes a Bogoliubov transformation $U$ and a normalized state $\phi \in {\mathcal F}_n$ such that 
$\widehat{E}_1=\langle \phi|U^\dag HU |\phi\rangle$. The state  $\phi$ is succinctly specified as superposition
of $ \exp[O(m\log(m/\varepsilon))]$ Fock basis vectors.
\end{theorem}
It suffices to consider $m\leq n$, since otherwise direct
computation in the full Fock space takes time
$2^{O(n)}\leq2^{O(m)}$, within the claimed bounds.
For a constant impurity size $m=O(1)$ and the interaction Hamiltonian satisfying $\|V\|\le \poly(n)$, we obtain a polynomial-time algorithm i.e., the runtime is $\poly(n,1/\varepsilon)$. For comparison, the previously best known algorithm of~\cite{bravyi2017complexity} has runtime scaling exponentially with $m\log^3{(m/\varepsilon)}$. 
We note that recently Jiang~\emph{et al.}\ announced a polynomial-time {\em quantum} algorithm approximating the ground energy of impurity models~\cite{jiang2026impuritybqp}.
Our classical algorithm borrows some ideas of~\cite{jiang2026impuritybqp} such as the Krylov subspaces, see Section~\ref{sec:ground-energy-proof} for details. 

\paragraph{Thermofield-double approximation.}

Our second result concerns the thermal equilibrium properties of quantum impurity models. 
Let $\beta \ge 0$ be the inverse temperature and  $\rho_\beta$ be the thermal Gibbs state
\[
\rho_\beta = \frac{e^{-\beta H}}{ \mathrm{Tr} \left( e^{-\beta H} \right)}
\]
with the canonical purification
\[
    \lvert\mathsf{TFD}_\beta\rangle
    \in\mathcal F_n\otimes\mathcal F_n
    \cong\mathcal F_{2n},
\]
which is often referred to as the \emph{Thermofield Double  state} (see  Section~\ref{sec:tfd-preliminaries} for a formal definition). Our second result shows that this purification can be approximated by a short superposition of fermionic Gaussian states. 
\begin{theorem}[Gaussian spanning set]\label{thm:rank}
Let $\delta \in (0,1)$. Fix a bath Hamiltonian $H_0$ and an impurity support $\cal I$ as above. For any  inverse temperature $\beta\ge 0$, there exists a Bogoliubov unitary  $U_\beta\, : \, \calF_{2n}\to \calF_{2n}$ and a set of Fock configurations
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-main}
\mathcal X_{\beta,\delta} \subseteq \{0,1\}^{2n}, \qquad 
 |\mathcal X_{\beta,\delta}|  \le  (2+\beta)^{O(m)}/\delta
\end{equation}
such that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:TFD_approx}
\sum_{x\in \mathcal X_{\beta,\delta}} |\langle  \mathsf{TFD}_\beta|U_\beta|x\rangle|^2 \ge 1-\delta^2
\end{equation}
for all interaction Hamiltonians $V$ supported on ${\cal I}$. The Bogoliubov transformation $U_\beta$ and the set $\mathcal X_{\beta,\delta}$ can be computed in time $\poly(n,1+\beta)$ and $\poly(n,1+\beta,1/\delta)$ respectively, where the degree of polynomials may depend on $m$.
\end{theorem}
Here $U_\beta$ depends only on $H_0,{\cal I},\beta$, while $\mathcal X_{\beta,\delta}$ additionally depends on the accuracy $\delta$. Neither depends on the interaction Hamiltonian $V$ and no bound on $\norm{V}$ is required. Theorem~\ref{thm:rank} implies that $|\mathsf{TFD}_\beta\rangle$ can be approximated by a superposition of states
$U_\beta|x\rangle$ with $x\in \mathcal X_{\beta,\delta}$ but does not specify the coefficients in this superposition. In the next theorem, we show that these coefficients  can be efficiently computed as well under an additional norm bound $\|V\|\le 1$. This provides an efficient classical algorithm for computing a low-rank superposition of Gaussian states approximating the thermofield double state. 
\begin{theorem}[Constructive TFD approximation]\label{ct:main}
Suppose $\norm{V}\le1$.
For  $\beta\ge0$ and $\delta \in (0,1/2)$,
let $U_\beta\, : \, \calF_{2n}\to \calF_{2n}$ and $\mathcal X_{\beta,\delta}\subseteq \{0,1\}^{2n}$ be the  Bogoliubov transformation and  the set of Fock configurations of Theorem~\ref{thm:rank}. There is a classical algorithm  that computes a set of coefficients $\{c_x \in \C \, : \, x\in \mathcal X_{\beta,\delta}\}$ such that  $\sum_{x\in  \mathcal X_{\beta,\delta}} |c_x|^2=1$ and 
\[
\left\| 
|\mathsf{TFD}_\beta\rangle - \sum_{x\in \mathcal X_{\beta,\delta}} c_x U_\beta |x\rangle \right\| \le C\delta
\]
for a universal constant $C>0$.
The algorithm has runtime
\[
 \poly(n,1+\beta,1/\delta)
 \exp\!\left[O\!\left(m\log\frac{m(1+\beta)}{\delta}\right)\right].
\]
\end{theorem}
Thus, for constant $m$, the above algorithm has runtime polynomial in $n,\beta,1/\delta$. 
Theorem~\ref{ct:main} allows us to approximate Gibbs-state expectation values of observables given as sums of polynomially
many monomials in the 
Majorana operators $a_j+a_j^\dagger$
and $i(a_j-a_j^\dagger)$. Their matrix elements between the
Gaussian states in the TFD approximation can be computed
efficiently using the generalized Wick theorem
of~\cite{bravyi2017complexity}.
For an observable $P$, the resulting additive error in approximating $\mathrm{Tr}(\rho_\beta P)$ is at most $2C\delta \|P\|$, where $\delta$ is the error parameter of  Theorem~\ref{ct:main},
see Section~\ref{ct:thermodynamics}.
Finally, using Theorem~\ref{ct:main},
we can obtain an estimate of the Helmholtz free energy of quantum impurity models.
\begin{corollary}[Free-energy estimation]\label{ct:free-energy}
There is a classical algorithm that takes as input an impurity model Hamiltonian $H=H_0+V$ with
$\norm{V}\le1$, an inverse temperature $\beta>0$, and an
error tolerance $0<\varepsilon\le1/2$, and computes a real
number $F_{\rm out}$ satisfying
\[
 \left|F_{\rm out}-\mathsf F_\beta\right|\le\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 \mathsf F_\beta=-\frac1\beta\log\Tr e^{-\beta H}.
\]
The algorithm has runtime
\[
 \poly(n,1+\beta,\varepsilon^{-1})
 \exp\!\left[
 O\!\left(m\log\frac{m(1+\beta)}{\varepsilon}\right)
 \right],
\]
which is polynomial in $n$, $1+\beta$, and $\varepsilon^{-1}$
for any constant impurity size $m$.
\end{corollary}

\paragraph{Universal quantum computation.}
Our final result demonstrates that 
the time evolution generated by quantum impurity models can simulate a universal quantum computation with at most polynomial slowdown. 
The matchgate constructions of Brod and Childs~\cite{brod2014computational} imply universality for time-dependent impurity Hamiltonians with constant impurity size. Pham and Santos~\cite{pham2026time} obtained a time-independent construction with $m=O(S\log S)$ impurity modes for circuit depth $S$. 
Our construction, by combining the fixed, autonomous update rule of quantum Turing-machine models \cite{Deutsch1985,BernsteinVazirani1997} with fermionic quantum-walk and scattering computation \cite{childs2013universal}, achieves BQP-universal dynamics with a constant-size impurity and no external control.

\begin{theorem}[Universal quantum computation]
\label{thm:main-reduction}
There exists a fixed, number-conserving quartic interaction $V_{\mathcal I}$ supported on a fixed set $\mathcal I$ of $24$ fermionic modes and a fixed output mode $o\in\mathcal I$ with the following property.
Let $\mathcal C$ be a quantum circuit on $k\ge1$ qubits with $g$ gates from the universal gate set $\{H,T,\operatorname{CZ}\}$\footnote{Alternatively, we may use the universal two-qubit gate in \cite{barenco1995universal}, decreasing the impurity size to 16.}, and let
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qc}
p_{\mathcal C}=\expval{\mathcal C^\dagger (\ketbra{0})_{k}\, \mathcal C}{0^k}
\end{equation}
be the probability of measuring $0$ on its output qubit after applying $\mathcal C$ to $\ket{0^k}$.
Then one can construct, by a deterministic classical algorithm running in time polynomial in $k+g$,
a quadratic bath Hamiltonian $H_0=\sum_{j,\ell=1}^n h_{jl}a_j^\dagger a_\ell$ with $h=h^\dagger$ and $\norm{h}\le2$,
an explicitly specified Slater determinant $\ket{\Psi}\in\mathcal F_n$,
and a positive integer evolution time $T$, such that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:main-reduction}
\Bigl|\langle\Psi|e^{i(H_0+V_{\mathcal I})T}a_o^\dagger a_o\,
e^{-i(H_0+V_{\mathcal I})T}|\Psi\rangle-p_{\mathcal C}\Bigr|\le\frac1{12},
\qquad n,T=O\bigl((k+g)^{4}\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

We note that the interaction $V_{\mathcal I}$ and output mode $o$ are identical for every instance, and the information of the circuit $\mathcal C$ is encoded into the initial state $\ket{\Psi}$.
As a corollary, estimating the occupation of the output mode $o$ after time evolution under a quantum impurity Hamiltonian is $\mathsf{BQP}$-hard, and the associated promise problem is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete; containment in $\mathsf{BQP}$ follows from standard Hamiltonian simulation.

\begin{corollary}[BQP-hardness]\label{cor:bqp}
For $V_{\mathcal I}$ and $o$ as in \Cref{thm:main-reduction}, consider the following problem:
given $H_0$, $\ket{\Psi}$ and $T$ as above, with $T$ bounded by a polynomial in the input length,
estimate
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:occupation}
\langle\Psi|e^{i(H_0+V_{\mathcal I})T}a_o^\dagger a_o\,
e^{-i(H_0+V_{\mathcal I})T}|\Psi\rangle
\end{equation}
to additive error $1/12$ with success probability at least $2/3$.
This estimation problem is $\mathsf{BQP}$-hard, and the associated promise problem of deciding whether \eqref{eq:occupation} is at least $2/3$ or at most $1/3$ is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Technical overview I: equilibrium algorithms}
In this section we give a brief overview of the classical algorithms for equilibrium.

\subsubsection{Ground energy estimation}
Here we sketch main ideas used to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:ground-energy-algorithm} which gives an efficient classical algorithm for ground-energy estimation of fermionic Hamiltonians with impurities. Given an input impurity Hamiltonian, we identify a small set of Fock configurations whose span contains a state of nearly optimal energy and prove that these configurations can be efficiently enumerated. Diagonalizing the Hamiltonian restricted to this span then gives the desired ground-energy estimate. Our approach shares structural similarities with ideas used in numerical renormalization group and block Lanczos methods for impurity models~\cite{bulla2008numerical,shirakawa2014block}.
We illustrate the associated main ideas in Figure~\ref{fig:impurity-shell-krylov} and describe them below. 

The impurity Hamiltonian can be brought into the following canonical form after applying a Bogoliubov transformation and a known shift by a multiple of the identity (see e.g.,~\cite{terhal2002classical,bravyi2017complexity})
\begin{equation}\label{eq:H0_after_Bogo}
H = H_0 + V, \quad H_0=\sum_{j=1}^n e_j \beta_j^\dagger \beta_j = d\Gamma(h), \quad h = \mathrm{diag}(e_1,\ldots,e_n), \quad 0\le e_j\le 1.    
\end{equation}
Here, $d\Gamma(h)$ denotes the quadratic (free) Hamiltonian associated with the one-particle matrix $h$. For a vector $z\in \C^n$, let $\beta(z) = \sum_{j=1}^n \overline{z}_j \beta_j$ be the annihilation operator of the one-particle direction $z$. 
 Each original mode is a linear combination $a_j=\beta(w_j)+\beta(w_j')^\dagger$ for some vectors $w_j,w_j'\in\C^n$. By assumption, $V$ is a polynomial in $a_j,a_j^\dagger$ with $j\in\mathcal I$, hence an even Hermitian polynomial in $\beta(w)$ and $\beta(w)^\dagger$ with $w$ in the \emph{impurity subspace}
 \begin{equation}
 \label{eq:one-particle-directions}
\Aimp:=\Span{\left\{w_j,w_j' : j\in\mathcal I\right\}}.
 \end{equation}
 By definition, $m=2|\mathcal I|$ and thus
$\dim{\Aimp}\le m$. We can assume without loss of generality that 
\[
\dim{\Aimp}=m
\]
by extending $\Aimp$ arbitrarily to an $m$-dimensional subspace, if necessaary.

Even though $V$ is supported only on one-particle directions from $\Aimp$, the quadratic Hamiltonian $H_0$ can nevertheless couple $\Aimp$ to additional bath directions. The challenge is to determine which additional bath directions and simultaneous occupations to retain so that the resulting subspace contains a state of nearly optimal energy.

\paragraph{Opening an artificial bath gap.}
The first obstacle is that the bath $H_0$ may contain arbitrarily many low-energy modes. To reduce this dimension, we can choose to only keep those configurations below a given bath-energy threshold. However, this still may retain exponentially many configurations since many modes can be occupied independently while their total energy remains below the threshold. Restricting instead to configurations with at most a fixed number of particles reduces the dimension, but may discard relevant configurations since low bath energy does not imply low particle number. 
To keep both the retained space small and control the error in the ground energy, we thus choose to regularize the bath energies instead of truncating the Fock space. We achieve this by fixing a parameter $\omega = \varepsilon/(4m)$ given a desired accuracy $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and then replacing $e_j$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:H0_after_Bogo} by
$$
\widetilde{e}_j := \max\{e_j,\omega\},
$$
and defining the modified bath Hamiltonian denoted by $\widetilde{H}_0$ and that including the impurity interaction $V$, denoted by $\widetilde{H}$, as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gap_Hamiltonians}
\widetilde H_0 = \sum_j \widetilde{e}_j \beta_j^\dagger \beta_j, \qquad \widetilde H=\widetilde H_0+V .
\end{equation}
Denoting the new one-particle matrix as $\widetilde{h} = \mathrm{diag}(\widetilde{e}_1,\ldots,\widetilde{e}_n)$ so that $\widetilde{H}_0 = d\Gamma(\widetilde{h})$, we immediately observe that $\omega \Id \preceq \widetilde h\preceq I$. The bath is thus now gapped but still contains all $n$ modes.
Note also that $H\preceq \widetilde H$.

Moreover, we prove that the ground-state energy of this modified Hamiltonian is still a good approximation of the true energy $E_1(H)$. Particularly, we show in Lemma~\ref{ge:rounding-lemma} (in Section~\ref{sec:ground-energy-proof}) that
$$
0 \leq E_1(\widetilde H)-E_1(H) \leq m\omega = \varepsilon/4.
$$
Note that the approximation error only depends on the impurity dimension and not on the number of low-energy bath modes. This is due to the fact that among the bath directions whose original energies are
below $\omega$, only the projection of the impurity subspace $\Aimp$ can participate nontrivially in the interaction, and this projection has dimension at most \(m\).  All orthogonal low-energy directions are free zero-energy modes after temporarily setting these energies to zero, and a ground state may be chosen with all such modes empty.  Thus only an \(m\)-dimensional collection of low-energy directions can incur the rounding cost.  

\paragraph{Energy shells and the enlarged boundary.}
The next step is to exploit the fact that the impurity, which acts only through the subspace $\Aimp$ of dimension at most $m$, also only sees a few directions at each energy scale. We partition the spectrum of $\widetilde{h}$ into dyadic intervals
\[
[\omega,2\omega),\ [2\omega,4\omega),\ [4\omega,8\omega),\ldots ,
\]
Specifically, we define energy \emph{shells}
$$
I_s := [\omega_s, 2\omega_s) \quad \text{where} \quad \omega_s := 2^s \omega, \forall s = 0,\ldots, S-1,
$$
with $S = O(\log(1/\omega)) = O\!\left(\log{m}/{\varepsilon}\right)$. Let $\mathcal{H}_s$ be the corresponding spectral subspaces of the single-body Hilbert space and let $\Pi_s$ denote the orthogonal projector onto $\mathcal{H}_s$. Note that we simply bin the spectrum of $\widetilde{h}$ and do not replace the energies within a shell by a common value. A shell may contain many modes but the interaction $V$ sees at most $m$ directions in it. We define the shell boundary $\A_s$, which is the portion of a given shell $s$ accessible to the impurity interaction, as
\begin{equation}\label{def:shell_boundary}
\A_s := \Pi_s \Aimp \subseteq\mathcal H_s
   \end{equation}
where $\Aimp$ is the impurity subspace defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:one-particle-directions}. As $\dim \Aimp = m$, we have  $\dim \A_s\le m$. The corresponding orthogonal complement $\B_s$ is then
\[
\B_s := \mathcal{H}_s \ominus \A_s = \mathcal{H}_s \cap \A_s^\perp,
\]
which we call the \emph{residual bath} and where $\ominus$ denotes the orthogonal complement within the indicated space. Thus, $\mathcal H_s=\mathcal{A}_s\oplus \mathcal{B}_s$. Modes in \(\mathcal{B}_s\) do not appear directly in the interaction,
although they may still influence the impurity indirectly through the
quadratic bath Hamiltonian. Taking direct sums over all shells gives
\[
\A=\bigoplus_s \A_s, \qquad \B=\bigoplus_s \B_s,
\]
with $ \dim \A \leq mS = O\!\left(m\log {m}/{\varepsilon}\right)$. Thus all interacting degrees of freedom have been collected into a small one-particle boundary \(\A\), while the potentially large remainder \(\B\) is free except for its coupling to this boundary. Relative to \(\A\oplus \B\), the rounded one-particle Hamiltonian has block
form
\[
\widetilde h =
\begin{pmatrix}
    h_{\A} &T\\
    T^\dagger & E
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(E=\bigoplus_sE_s\) acts within the residual bath and
\(T=\bigoplus_sT_s\) couples the residual bath to the boundary.
If shell \(s\) contains energies in \([\omega_s,2\omega_s]\), then
Lemma~\ref{ge:block-lemma} shows that
\[
    \omega_sI\preceq E_s\preceq2\omega_sI,
    \qquad
    \|T_s\|\le \frac{\omega_s}{2}.
\]
These bounds use only that the energies within a shell differ by at most a
factor of two. At the many-body level, the same decomposition takes the schematic form
\[
    \widetilde H
    =
    H_A
    +
    b^\dagger E b
    +
    a^\dagger T b
    +
    b^\dagger T^\dagger a.
\]
Here the fermionic modes \(a_\ell\) span the boundary \(\mathcal{A}\), the modes
\(b_j\) span the residual bath \(\mathcal{B}\), and
\[
    n_A:=\dim \mathcal{A}\le mS.
\]
The operator \(H_A\), which contains the full interaction \(V\), acts only
on the boundary modes.  The term \(b^\dagger E b\) describes free evolution
within the residual bath, while
\[
    a^\dagger T b+b^\dagger T^\dagger a
\]
contains the only couplings between the residual bath and the interacting
boundary. This decomposition suggests the central question of the proof:
\emph{which of the many residual-bath directions can actually influence the
interacting ground state, and how strongly can they do so?} To answer this, we use a decomposition of the residual bath closely related to Lanczos-based constructions used in numerical impurity solvers~\cite{busser2013lanczos,shirakawa2014block}.

\paragraph{Krylov depth.}
The residual bath \(\B_s=\mathcal H_s\ominus \A_s\) may still have dimension
\(\Theta(n)\), but its directions need not be equally relevant.  Since the
interaction acts only through the boundary \(\A_s\), a residual-bath mode can
influence the impurity only by communicating with that boundary. The map
\[
T_s^\dagger : \A_s \to \B_s
\]
identifies the bath directions that couple directly to \( \A_s\), namely
$\operatorname{Im}(T_s^\dagger)$.  Once inside the residual bath, further propagation is governed entirely by the free bath Hamiltonian \(E_s\).  It is therefore natural to organize \(\B_s\) according to how many applications of \(E_s\) are needed to generate
a new direction starting from \(\operatorname{Im}(T_s^\dagger)\). For an integer \(\ell\ge0\), define the block Krylov space~\cite{golub2013matrix}
\[
    \mathcal K_{s,\ell}
    :=
    \operatorname{span}
    \bigl\{
        E_s^jT_s^\dagger u:
        u\in \A_s,\ 0\le j<\ell
    \bigr\},
    \qquad
    \mathcal K_{s,0}:=\{0\}.
\]
They are subspaces of $\mathcal B_s$. In particular,
\[
    \mathcal K_{s,1}
    =
    \operatorname{Im}(T_s^\dagger)
\]
contains precisely the bath directions coupled directly to the boundary,
while \(\mathcal K_{s,2}\) additionally contains the new directions obtained
after one application of \(E_s\), and so on.  The genuinely new directions
appearing at step \(\ell+1\) form the orthogonal layer
\[
    {\mathcal W}_{s,\ell}
    :=
    \mathcal K_{s,\ell+1}
    \ominus
    \mathcal K_{s,\ell}.
\]
We call \(\ell\) the \emph{Krylov depth}.  It is an algebraic, rather than
spatial, notion of distance from the impurity: a direction at large depth is
one that can only be reached after repeatedly propagating the
boundary--bath coupling through the free bath Hamiltonian. Because the initial space
\(\operatorname{Im}(T_s^\dagger)\) has dimension at most \(m\), each new
Krylov layer also has dimension at most \(m\):
\[
    \dim {\mathcal W}_{s,\ell}\le m.
\]
Hence across all shells there are at most
$mS$ 
bath modes at any fixed depth.  More importantly, if
\(v\in {\mathcal W}_{s,\ell}\), then orthogonality to all shallower Krylov spaces gives
\[
    T_sE_s^jv=0,
    \qquad
    0\le j<\ell.
\]
The formal Krylov construction and these properties are given in
Section~\ref{sec:blockkrylov}. 
Thus a depth-\(\ell\) mode cannot couple to the boundary through fewer than $\ell$ applications of $E_s$.

This is exactly the structural information we need, but by itself it is
only a one-particle statement.  To obtain an algorithm we must convert
Krylov depth into a statement about the occupation of these modes in the
actual interacting many-body ground state.

\paragraph{From Krylov depth to ground-state occupation.}
Let \(\psi\) be a normalized ground state of \(\widetilde H\). For $v \in \mathcal{B}$ and $\norm{v}=1$, let $b(v) := \beta(v)$ where we write $b$ to emphasize that it belongs to the residual bath.
Since a fermionic mode can have occupation only \(0\) or \(1\), the operator $n_v:=b(v)^\dagger b(v)$ has eigenvalues \(0\) and \(1\). Therefore, for any state \(\psi\),
\[
\langle\psi|n_v|\psi\rangle
=
\langle\psi|b(v)^\dagger b(v)|\psi\rangle
=
\|b(v)\psi\|^2.
\]
Thus \(\|b(v)\psi\|^2\) is exactly the probability that the mode \(v\)
is occupied in the state \(\psi\), referred to as the occupation probability of the fermionic mode \(v\). It remains to understand how likely a given bath mode is to be occupied in the interacting ground state. 
 To this end,  we must keep track of all the ways in which the free bath Hamiltonian
can propagate \(v\) into a direction visible to the boundary.  This is captured by the imaginary-time evolution
\[
    e^{-tE}v
    =
    v-tEv+\frac{t^2}{2}E^2v-\cdots.
\]
Applying $T$ then extracts components that couple back into the boundary, i.e.,  $\|Te^{-tE}v\|_2$
measures the strength with which the bath direction \(v\), after evolving under the free residual-bath Hamiltonian for imaginary time \(t\), couples
to the impurity-facing boundary.
 This naturally leads us to define
\[
    s(v)
    :=
    \int_0^\infty
    \|Te^{-tE}v\|\,dt,
\]
which measures the total effective coupling of the bath direction \(v\) to
the boundary over imaginary time. The usefulness of the Krylov decomposition is that this quantity decays
exponentially with depth.  More precisely, Lemma~\ref{ge:depth} proves that
for every unit vector \(v\in\mathcal W_{s,\ell}\),
\begin{align}
\label{eq:boundons}
    s(v)
    \le
    \frac12\,3^{-\ell},
\end{align}
while \(s(v)=0\) for completely decoupled bath directions. The reason for this decay is already visible from the Krylov construction.
If \(v\in\mathcal W_{s,\ell}\), then
\[
    T_sE_s^jv=0,
    \qquad
    0\le j<\ell.
\]
Consequentially,
\[
T_se^{-tE_s}v
=
\sum_{j=0}^\infty
\frac{(-t)^j}{j!}T_sE_s^jv = \sum_{j \geq \ell} \frac{(-t)^j}{j!}T_sE_s^jv
\]
as the first \(\ell\) terms vanish.  Thus a depth-\(\ell\) mode can couple back
to the boundary only through terms involving at least \(\ell\) powers of
\(E_s\).  Using the fact that the energies within a shell differ by at most
a factor of two gives the exponential bound in Eq.~\eqref{eq:boundons}. The full calculation is
given in Section~\ref{sec:krylovdecay}.  Thus, Krylov depth has the desired operational meaning: bath modes
far from the boundary in Krylov depth are exponentially unlikely to be
occupied in the interacting ground state.

A one-mode bound, however, is not enough to control the full many-body state:
there are exponentially many Fock configurations, and a configuration may
contain several individually unlikely bath modes.  To truncate the Fock space,
we therefore need a bound on the probability that an arbitrary collection of
bath modes is occupied simultaneously.

\paragraph{Multiparticle pull-through.}
To convert the one-particle decay above into control of the many-body
ground state, we use the multiparticle pull-through lemma, see Lemma~\ref{ge:pull}. Intuitively, a pull-through identity moves bath annihilation operators through the imaginary-time evolution, replacing each of them by an integrated source acting on the impurity-facing boundary.  Let \(\psi\) be a normalized global ground state of \(\widetilde H\). 
We show in Lemma~\ref{ge:pull} that for any one-particle directions $v_1,\ldots,v_p$, 
\[
\|b(v_1)\cdots b(v_p)\psi\| \le \prod_{i=1}^p s(v_i).
\]
The proof is given in Section~\ref{sec:pullthrough}. Consequently, if $v_1,\ldots,v_p$ are orthonormal vectors such that $v_j$ belong to a Krylov layer of depth $\ell(j)$,  the corresponding number operators $n_j =b(v_j)^\dagger b(v_j)$  obey
\[
\left\langle\psi\middle|
    \prod_{j=1}^p n_j
\middle|\psi\right\rangle
\le
\prod_{j=1}^p s(v_j)^2\leq      \prod_{j=1}^p
\left(\frac14\,9^{-\ell(j)}\right),
\]
where the second inequality follows from Eq.~\eqref{eq:boundons}. 
Thus not only is each deep mode unlikely to be occupied; simultaneous
occupation of several deep modes is suppressed by the product of their
individual penalties. This product structure is what finally lets us control the exponentially
large set of Fock configurations.  Rather than truncating at a fixed Krylov
depth, we assign a cost to each occupied mode and bound the total cost.

\paragraph{Weighted Fock-space truncation.}
The joint occupation bound suggests a natural many-body truncation. For a layer mode at Krylov depth $\ell$, the occupation probability is suppressed exponentially in $\ell$, and the penalties multiply for simultaneous occupations.  Thus, after taking logarithms, the relevant quantity is an \emph{additive} cost over all occupied bath modes, rather than the maximum Krylov depth appearing in the configuration. 

Let $\{v_i\}_{i \in [n]}$ be an orthonormal one-particle basis over the boundary $\mathcal{A}$, all non-zero Krylov layers $\mathcal{W}_{s,\ell}$ and the decoupled remainder bath subspace. Let $J \subseteq [n]$ be the indices of the Krylov-layer vectors. For $j \in J$, let $\ell(j)$ denote the depth of the layer containing $v_j$ and let $n_j := b(v_j)^\dagger b(v_j)$ denote its occupation. 
Let $U$ be the Bogoliubov transformation mapping the original Fock
basis $\{\ket{x}\}$ to the occupation basis of the constructed modes.
Thus $U\ket{x}$ has occupation $x_j$ in the mode associated with
$v_j$.
We then define the weighted occupation operator
\[
Q := \sum_{j\in J} (\ell(j)+1)n_j,
\]
where the extra $+1$ also penalizes the number of bath excitations, so that many simultaneous occupations at shallow depth are not retained for free.  Boundary occupations are left completely unrestricted.
 
For a Fock configuration $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ in this basis, where $x_j$ is the occupation of $v_j$, let
\[
Q(x) := \sum_{j\in J}(\ell(j)+1)x_j,
\]
and for an integer cutoff $R\ge 0$ define
\[
\mathcal{X}_R
:=
\left\{
    x\in\{0,1\}^n:
    Q(x)\le R,\quad
    x_j=0\ \text{for every decoupled mode }j
\right\}.
\]
Let $P_R$ project onto the span of $\{U\ket{x}:x\in \mathcal{X}_R\}$, that is,
\[
 P_R=U\left(\sum_{x\in \mathcal{X}_R}\ket{x}\bra{x}\right)U^\dagger,
\]
and write $    p_R:=\|(I-P_R)\psi\|^2,$ and 
$    D_R:=|\mathcal{X}_R|=\operatorname{rank}(P_R).$ 
Thus $p_R$ is the ground-state probability mass discarded by the
truncation, while $D_R$ is the dimension of the retained many-body
space. In Section~\ref{sec:weightfoctruncation}, we give the two complementary estimates
\begin{align}
\label{eq:boundonpR}
    p_R\le e^{mS}3^{-R},
    \qquad
    D_R\le e^{(\log 2+1/2)mS}3^R.
\end{align}
The first follows by bounding an exponential moment of $Q$ using the 
joint occupation estimates and then applying Markov's inequality.
The second is the corresponding weighted counting argument for the
number of configurations satisfying $Q(x)\le R$. The important point is that we do \emph{not} keep all configurations
supported on the first $R$ Krylov layers.  Such a cutoff would ignore
the additional suppression of configurations containing many
simultaneous excitations.  Instead, we constrain their total weighted
Krylov cost.  Hence increasing $R$ exponentially suppresses the
discarded ground-state mass while increasing the retained dimension
by only an exponential factor in $R$.  This is the main compression
step of the proof.

\paragraph{From norm truncation to energy truncation.}
The fact that $p_R$ is small does not by itself imply that the energy
changes little, since $\|\widetilde H\|$ may grow with $n$.  The
particular truncation above has an additional useful property: it does
not restrict the boundary modes.  Since the interaction $V$ is
supported entirely on the boundary, $[P_R,V]=0$. 

Let
$   N=\sum_j \beta_j^\dagger \beta_j
$  
be the total quasiparticle-number operator in the basis used above.
Every retained configuration contains at most $mS$ boundary particles
and at most $R$ Krylov-layer particles, because every occupied layer
mode contributes at least one unit to $Q$.  Therefore
\[
    \|NP_R\|\le mS+R.
\]
Since the rounded one-particle energies satisfy
$    0\le \widetilde e_j\le 1,$ 
we have $   0\preceq \widetilde H_0\preceq N,
$ and 
$ \|\widetilde H_0P_R\|\le mS+R.$  Now define the normalized projected state
\[
    \phi_R
    :=
    \frac{P_R\psi}{\sqrt{1-p_R}}.
\]
Using the ground-state equation together with $[P_R,V]=0$ gives
\[
    0
    \le
    \langle\phi_R|\widetilde H|\phi_R\rangle
    -
    E_1(\widetilde H)
    \le
    \frac{\sqrt{p_R}}{1-p_R}(mS+R).
\]
This is proved in Section~\ref{sec:groundenergyapprox}.  Notice in
particular that the bound is independent of $\|V\|$: the interaction
term cancels exactly because $P_R$ commutes with $V$. We now choose the cutoff exactly as in the formal proof, $R=O(mS+\log 1/\varepsilon)$
 and plugging this with the upper bound on $p_R$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:boundonpR}, we have
\[
    0
    \le
    \langle\phi_R|\widetilde H|\phi_R\rangle
    -
    E_1(\widetilde H)
    \le {\varepsilon}/{4}.
\]
Similarly plugging this into Eq.~\eqref{eq:boundonpR}, we also have $D_R\leq \exp(O(m\log (m/\varepsilon)))$.
 Thus the original $2^n$-dimensional ground-energy problem has been
reduced to an explicitly defined subspace whose dimension is
$(m/\varepsilon)^{O(m)}$, and hence polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$ for
constant impurity size $m$.
\paragraph{The algorithm.}
It remains to show that the retained space and the restriction of the
Hamiltonian to it can be constructed efficiently.  This is carried out
in Section~\ref{ge:algorithm}.

Set $\omega=\varepsilon/(4m)$, $R=O(mS+\log 1/\varepsilon)$. 
Starting from the compact description of the input Hamiltonian, we
construct the rounded bath energies, the dyadic shells and their
boundary spaces, and the full ordered basis of boundary, Krylov-layer,
and decoupled modes. Only boundary modes and Krylov layers of depth
less than $R$ can be occupied in the retained space; all other modes
are required to be empty.
The full basis and the induced action of $U$ on the modes can be
computed in polynomial time in $n$ and the relevant parameters.
We enumerate the configurations in $\mathcal{X}_R=\{x_1,\ldots,x_{D_R}\}$
and form the compression of the original Hamiltonian,
\[
    B_{\mu\nu}
    :=
    \bra{x_\mu}U^\dagger HU\ket{x_\nu} .
\]
The quadratic contribution is obtained directly from the retained
matrix elements of the original one-particle Hamiltonian $h$.
The interaction $V$ acts only on the
boundary and is given by its compact impurity description, so its
matrix elements can also be computed without ever constructing the
full $2^n\times2^n$ Hamiltonian.  Importantly, the entire retained
basis is determined from the input Hamiltonian alone; the unknown
ground state $\psi$ is used only in the analysis.

Finally, we compute a normalized approximate lowest eigenvector $z$
of $B$, with $z^\dagger Bz\le E_1(B)+\varepsilon/4$.
Here $E_1(B)$ is the smallest eigenvalue of $B$.
Define the sparse state in the original occupation basis by
\[
 \ket\phi=\sum_{\mu=1}^{D_R}z_\mu\ket{x_\mu},
 \qquad U\ket\phi=\sum_{\mu=1}^{D_R}z_\mu U\ket{x_\mu},
\]
and return $U$, $\phi$, and
\[
 \widehat E_1=z^\dagger Bz
 =\bra\phi U^\dagger HU\ket\phi.
\]
The projected ground state $\phi_R$ is a variational witness for $B$.
Using $H\preceq\widetilde H$, the truncation bound, and the rounding
bound gives
\begin{align*}
 E_1(H)\leq E_1(B)
 &\leq\bra{\phi_R}H\ket{\phi_R}
 \leq\bra{\phi_R}\widetilde H\ket{\phi_R}\\
 &\leq E_1(\widetilde H)+\varepsilon/4
 \leq E_1(H)+\varepsilon/2.
\end{align*}
The eigensolver bound therefore implies
\[
 E_1(H)\leq\widehat E_1
 \leq E_1(H)+3\varepsilon/4\leq E_1(H)+\varepsilon,
\]
as claimed. The output $\phi$ is supported on $D_R$ original Fock
configurations, while $U\phi$ is the low-energy physical state.

Since $S=O(\log(m/\varepsilon))$, $R=O(m\log(m/\varepsilon))$, and $D_R
    =
    \exp\!\left[
        O\!\left(
            m\log {m}/{\varepsilon}
        \right)
    \right],$
all one-particle linear-algebra operations are polynomial in $n$ and
the relevant parameters, while constructing and diagonalizing the
projected many-body Hamiltonian costs polynomial time in $D_R$ and
$1+\|V\|$.  Section~\ref{ge:algorithm} gives the detailed arithmetic
complexity and yields the total runtime
\[
    \poly(n,1+\|V\|)
    \exp\!\left[
        O\!\left(
            m\log\frac{m}{\varepsilon}
        \right)
    \right].
\]
For constant impurity size $m$, this is polynomial in both $n$ and
$1/\varepsilon$.

\subsubsection{Gaussian spanning set for the TFD state}

Next we sketch the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:rank}, which constructs
a small Gaussian spanning set approximating the thermofield-double
state. The proof uses the Krylov decomposition and weighted truncation
ideas from the ground-energy proof, but applies them to excitations
relative to the TFD state of a certain free-fermion Hamiltonian.
 We first explain the choice of
annihilation operators that makes this possible.
Below we write $\rho_\beta(H)$ and 
$\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(H)}$ for the Gibbs state and the thermofield double state at the inverse temperature $\beta$ associated with a Hamiltonian $H$.

\paragraph{Free TFD state as a vacuum.}
Consider first a single fermionic mode $b,b^\dagger$ with a Hamiltonian
$\lambda b^\dagger b$, where $\lambda\ge0$.
The corresponding Gibbs state  at the inverse temperature $\beta$ is 
\[
\rho_\beta(\lambda b^\dagger b) = p_0 |0\rangle \langle 0| + p_1 |1\rangle \langle 1|
\]
where the occupation probabilities are 
\[
p_0 = \frac1{1+e^{-\beta\lambda}}   \quad \mbox{and} \quad p_1= \frac{e^{-\beta\lambda}}{1+e^{-\beta\lambda}}
\]
The corresponding TFD state  is defined as 
\[
 \ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(\lambda b^\dag b)}
 =\sqrt{p_0} \ket{00}-i\sqrt{p_1}\ket{11} \in {\cal F}_2.
\]
Here the second mode is an ancilla (environment) used for purifying the first (physical) mode.
The extra phase shift $-i$ follows 
the fermionic purification convention of Section~\ref{sec:tfd-preliminaries} and does not affect the physical Gibbs state.
By definition,  the Gibbs state is obtained from the TFD state by tracing out the ancillary mode.
Let $\widetilde b,\widetilde b^\dagger$ be the annihilation and creation operators on the ancillary mode.
The operators $b,\widetilde b$ obeys the canonical anticommutation rules. In particular, $b \widetilde b = - \widetilde b b$.

Define a pair of operators
\[
 \mathsf d_-=\sqrt{p_0}\, b+i\sqrt{p_1}\, \widetilde b^\dagger
 \quad\mbox{and}\quad
 \mathsf d_+=\sqrt{p_1}\, b^\dagger+i\sqrt{p_0}\, \widetilde b.
\]
One can check that $ \mathsf d_\pm$  annihilate the TFD state,
\[
 \mathsf d_\pm\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(\lambda b^\dag b)}=0.
\]
Besides, $\mathsf d_\pm$
satisfy the canonical anticommutation relations, that is,
\[
\{ \mathsf d_\eta, \mathsf d_{\eta'}\}=0  \quad \mbox{and} \quad 
\{ \mathsf d_\eta, \mathsf d^\dagger_{\eta'}\} =\delta_{\eta,\eta'} I.
\]
Thus the TFD state is equivalent to the vacuum state $|00\rangle$ modulo a basis change described
by a Bogoliubov transformation mapping $b,\widetilde b$ to $\mathsf d_+,\mathsf d_-$.
Informally, this basis change removes all  thermal fluctuations.

This construction naturally extends to any free fermion Hamiltonian.
Indeed, any such Hamiltonian can be diagonalized by a Bogoliubov transformation
and, up to additive scalar,  takes a form $H_{\mathrm{free}}=\sum_{j=1}^n \lambda_j b_j^\dagger b_j$,
where $\lambda_j\ge0$ and $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ are annihilation operators for $n$ fermionic modes.
The corresponding Gibbs state $\rho_\beta(H_{\mathrm{free}})$ is a product of $n$ single-mode Gibbs states
considered above and the  state $\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(H_{\mathrm{free}})}$
is defined by purifying each mode independently, see Section~\ref{sec:tfd-preliminaries} for details.
The state $\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(H_{\mathrm{free}})}$  is annihilated by $2n$  operators $\mathsf d_{\pm,j}$ such that 
$\mathsf d_{-,j}$ is a linear combination of $b_j$ and the corresponding ancillary mode operator $\widetilde b_j^\dagger$,
while $\mathsf d_{+,j}$ is a linear combination of $b_j^\dagger$ and $\widetilde b_j$.
The operators $\mathsf d_{\pm,j}$ with $j=1,\ldots,n$
obey the canonical anticommutation rules
and thus define a basis in which the state $\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(H_{\mathrm{free}})}$ becomes the vacuum $|0^{2n}\rangle$.
Informally, this basis change removes all  thermal fluctuations {\em in the absence of interactions}. 
We refer to the  operators  $\mathsf d_{\pm,j}$ as \emph{free TFD annihilators}. 

\paragraph{Exponential suppression of excitations.}
We express the interacting TFD
state $\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(H)}$ in the basis determined by the free TFD annihilators $\mathsf d_{\pm,j}$ associated with the residual bath Hamiltonian
$b^\dag E b$
used  in the ground state algorithm (with a few technical modifications).
The residual bath contains $n_B\le n$ modes, where $n_B$ depends on details of the Krylov decomposition.
These details are not essential for this high-level overview. 
The number operators $\mathsf d_{\pm,j}^\dagger\mathsf d_{\pm,j}$ with $j=1,\ldots,n_B$
count only  excitations caused by the interaction $V$ relative to the free TFD.
The crux of the proof is to control these  excitations and showing that joint occupations of modes at large Krylov depth
are exponentially suppressed. 
To this end we consider annihilators
\[
 \mathsf d_-(v)=\sum_{j=1}^{n_B}
                   \overline{\langle v_j,v\rangle}\mathsf d_{-,j}
 \quad \mbox{and} \quad
 \mathsf d_+(v)=\sum_{j=1}^{n_B}
                   \langle v_j,v\rangle \mathsf d_{+,j},
\]
where $v\in \B$ is an arbitrary vector in the one-particle space describing the residual bath
and $v_1,\ldots,v_{n_B}\in \B$ is the eigenbasis of $E$.
By definition, the operators $\mathsf d_{\pm}(v)$ annihilate the free TFD state $\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(b^\dag E b)}$.
We prove a thermal analogue of the multiparticle pull-through lemma showing that 
multiparticle excitations associated with the modes $\mathsf d_{\pm}(v)$ and the {\em interacting} TFD state are exponentially suppressed.
More formally,
\[
 \norm{\mathsf d_{\eta_1}(v_1)\cdots
       \mathsf d_{\eta_k}(v_k)\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(H)}}
 \leq\prod_{i=1}^k s_\beta(v_i)
\]
for arbitrary vectors $v_i\in\B$ and signs $\eta_i\in\{+,-\}$, where
\[
 s_\beta(v)=\int_0^{\beta/2}\norm{Te^{-tE}v}\,dt
\]
is a finite-temperature analogue of the integrated coupling used in the ground state algorithm. 
One technical difference is that the map $T$ coupling the residual bath $\B$ to the boundary $\A$ now
contains an extra thermal factor,
\[
T=h_{\A\B}(1+e^{-\beta E})^{-1/2}.
\]

For $\beta>0$, we
partition the bath spectrum into $S=O(\log(2+\beta))$ energy shells:
the low-energy interval $[0,\min\{1,\beta^{-1}\}]$ and disjoint
dyadic intervals above it.
The Krylov decomposition gives at most $m$ directions per shell
at each depth $\ell$, with
$s_\beta(v)\leq\frac12\,3^{-\ell}$ for every unit depth-$\ell$
vector. Each direction gives two free TFD modes, so there are at
most $2mS$ such modes at each depth. For any subset of distinct canonical modes
with number operators $\mathsf n_j$ and depths $\ell(j)$,
the pull-through lemma implies
\[
 \bra{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(H)}\prod_j\mathsf n_j
       \ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(H)}
 \leq\prod_j\left(\frac14\,9^{-\ell(j)}\right).
\]

\paragraph{Weighted truncation.}
Finally, we leave boundary occupations unrestricted and assign
cost $\ell+1$ to each occupied free TFD mode of depth $\ell$.
Together with the physical and ancillary boundary modes, the
free TFD modes define a Fock basis $\{U_\beta\ket{x}\}$, where $U_\beta$
is a Bogoliubov transformation. 
Projecting $\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(H)}$ onto the span of
configurations of total cost at most $R$, with all decoupled modes
empty, discards squared norm at most $e^{4mS}4^{-R}$ and retains
at most $e^{O(mS)}2^R$ configurations. Choosing

\subsubsection{Constructive approximation of the TFD state}

We now sketch the proof of Theorem~\ref{ct:main}, which computes
$\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(H)}$ as a linear
combination of states in the Gaussian spanning set of
Theorem~\ref{thm:rank}, assuming $\norm{V}\le1$.
The idea is to simulate Trotterized  imaginary time evolution 
of  $\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\tau(H)}$ over the interval $\tau \in [0,\beta]$
starting from  $\tau=0$.
The initial state $\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_0(H)}$
is an explicitly known Gaussian EPR-like state. 
We adapt the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:rank} to obtain
one $\tau$-independent Krylov decomposition.
At each time $\tau$, the corresponding free TFD annihilators
define a $\tau$-dependent Bogoliubov transformation $\mathcal U_\tau$
and a Fock basis $\{ \mathcal U_\tau |x\rangle\}$  such that 
$\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\tau(H)}$ 
has almost all its mass in the span of low-weight Fock configurations (weighted by the Krylov depth)
in the basis determined by $\mathcal U_\tau$.
We truncate all Fock configurations with the weight above certain cutoff $R$.
The truncated version of $\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\tau(H)}$ 
can be represented  succinctly by its coefficients in the chosen basis. 
We can also  efficiently compute matrix elements of $H$ needed 
to simulate each Trotter step, including 
the contribution from the time dependence of the basis.

The main challenge  is that imaginary  time evolution can amplify
errors. If we simply evolve and truncate at each Trotter step, the
per-step truncation errors
can accumulate into a large final error growing exponentially with $\beta$.
We avoid this problem by fitting the entire trajectory using
least squares. We fix the known initial state and determine
the coefficients at all subsequent Trotter  steps simultaneously,
minimizing the sum of squared errors in the Trotterized 
evolution. These errors include the components
outside the retained Gaussian span. The exact  trajectory  $\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\tau(H)}$,
after truncation, provides a good candidate for this fit with a small total residual. 
Therefore, the trajectory obtained by solving the least-squares problem also has a small total residual
and, in contrast to the exact trajectory, can be computed efficiently.

The key technical step is to prove that this small
residual implies a small error in the final state.
We show that the residuals lie in a small, explicitly computable enlargement
of the retained Gaussian span. We use H\"older's inequality for Schatten norms
to control
how much subsequent imaginary-time evolution can amplify
vectors in this enlarged span, while the thermal multiparticle pull-through lemma
makes the truncation errors small enough to compensate
for that amplification. We also need a computable rescaling
of the trajectory: an approximate ground energy, supplied by
Theorem~\ref{thm:ground-energy-algorithm}, and the free-bath
partition function keep the vector norms controlled without
requiring the unknown interacting partition function.
The rescaled trajectory satisfies a linear evolution equation,
so the fit is an ordinary linear least-squares problem.
Together,
these estimates give an algorithm that computes the final low-rank Gaussian approximation
of $\ket{\mathsf{TFD}_\beta(H)}$
 in time polynomial in $n$, $1+\beta$,
and $\delta^{-1}$ for fixed impurity size $m$.

title: Local random quantum circuits converge to the Porter-Thomas distribution in polynomial depth
abstract: Porter-Thomas statistics are a characteristic feature of the output distribution of random quantum states and, more broadly, chaotic quantum many-body systems. Convergence to Porter-Thomas plays a central role in random circuit sampling and experimental demonstrations of quantum advantage, where the output statistics of low-depth random quantum circuits are expected to be approximately Porter-Thomas, despite the absence of a rigorous proof of convergence. We show that the output distribution of polynomial-depth brickwork random circuits converges inverse-polynomially in total variation distance to the Porter-Thomas distribution. Specifically, consider the output probability distribution over a fixed bitstring of a local random quantum circuit, constructed from nearest-neighbor Haar random gates. Then, for any $m \geq 0$, the distribution corresponding to circuits of depth $O(n^{2m+1}\log(n))$ is at most $O(1/n^m)$ far in total variation distance from the Porter-Thomas distribution. Our proof uses moment bounds from approximate designs, analytic estimates for characteristic functions, and a local anticoncentration property for inverse moments.
summary:
**TL;DR** The authors prove the first rigorous statement that the output probability of a fixed bitstring, as a random variable over brickwork Haar random circuits, converges in total variation distance to the Porter–Thomas (exponential) distribution at polynomial depth: depth $O(n^{2m+1}\log n)$ gives TV distance $O(1/n^m)$. The proof combines $k$-design moment matching, a Hadamard three-circle argument in Fourier space, mollification, and a new inverse-moment/anticoncentration bound on the amplitude mass feeding into a single final-layer gate.

**The big picture** Random circuit sampling experiments and the cross-entropy benchmark used to validate them rest on the assumption that shallow random circuits produce output probabilities obeying the characteristic exponential statistics of fully chaotic dynamics. Until now this was supported only by numerics and by the weaker fact that finitely many moments match — and matching any finite number of moments provably does not pin down a distribution. This work closes the gap for brickwork circuits, showing genuine convergence in a strong distance measure at polynomial depth, by exploiting circuit structure in addition to moment information.

**Key contributions**
- A rigorous convergence theorem: depth-$\ell$ brickwork circuits forming $d^{-k}$-approximate $k$-designs have $d_{\rm TV} \le O(\sqrt{\log k/k})$ from Porter–Thomas; with $k=\Theta(n^{2m}\log n)$ and $\ell=\Theta(n^{2m+1}\log n)$ this is $O(1/n^m)$.
- A technique for upgrading moment control to TV control, circumventing the Hausdorff-moment-problem obstruction, via a three-region Fourier decomposition.
- A smoothness bound $\|f'\|_{L^1}=O(d)$ for the output-probability density, reduced to an inverse-moment bound $\mathbb{E}[R^{-1}]=O(d)$ on the mass $R$ entering the final gate.
- A local anticoncentration statement $\Pr[R\le t/d]\le A t^{12/11}$, proved by iteratively "freeing" qubits through the last two layers and bounding negative moments of $\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)$ ratios ($M_{3/2}=8$ at $q=3/2$).

**How it works** Using a Bobkov-type inequality, TV distance is bounded by the $L^2$ norm of the difference of characteristic functions, with support length $L=2k/d$ from known tail bounds. For $|t|\le d/2$, Taylor expansion plus $\epsilon\le d^{-k}$ moment closeness gives $O(d/(k2^{2k}))$. For $|t|\ge d/h$, convolving both densities with a band-limited mollifier (e.g. $\mathrm{sinc}^4$) kills the Fourier tail at TV cost $h\|f'\|_{L^1}$ — hence the need for the derivative bound. The intermediate band is handled by mapping the half-plane $\mathrm{Re}\,s\ge -s_1 d$ to the unit disk and applying the three-circle theorem, yielding $\le de^{-\Omega(kh^2)}/h$. Optimizing $h\sim\sqrt{\log k/k}$ gives the result.

**Why it matters** This puts the standard Porter–Thomas assumption underlying LXEB, certified randomness protocols, and quantum-advantage claims on rigorous footing, and gives transferable tools (three-circle interpolation plus mollification) for converting design properties into distributional closeness.

**Caveats** The depth is far above the experimentally relevant log/linear regime — nontrivial TV requires superlinear depth, and the conjecture is that the bounds are loose. The result concerns the distribution over circuits for one fixed bitstring, not the empirical bitstring distribution of a single circuit. Noise is not treated (left as an explicit open question), the analysis is brickwork-specific, and the mollification theorem assumes a monotone decreasing, absolutely continuous density. Inverse-exponential TV bounds appear out of reach with these methods.

title: Sublinear-depth Quantum Simulation of Electrons with Atomic Orbitals
abstract: Discretizing electronic degrees of freedom into atomic orbitals is the default choice to accurately model electrons in molecules in a compact and flexible way. We consider the task of simulating such electronic structure models on a quantum computer for $N$ orbitals, keeping the number of orbitals per atom constant. Atomic orbitals give rise to Hamiltonians with potentially up to $\mathcal{O}(N^4)$ terms and little structure, which made it challenging to match the complexity of methods based on plane waves and real-space grids. In this work, we show that a Trotter step for atomic orbitals can be implemented in depth $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{polylog}(N))$ without ancillas by combining a rigorous treatment of orbital localization, a hierarchical Hamiltonian decomposition based on the Fast Multipole Method, and shallow quantum Fourier arithmetic circuits. By bounding the Trotter error, we obtain sublinear simulation depth, and our total gate count $N^{5/3 + o(1)}$ matches the best scaling known for any basis.

\author{Jakob Günther}

\begin{abstract}
Discretizing electronic degrees of freedom into atomic orbitals is the default choice to accurately model electrons in molecules in a compact and flexible way.
We consider the task of simulating such electronic structure models on a quantum computer for $\nsys$ orbitals, keeping the number of orbitals per atom constant.
Atomic orbitals give rise to Hamiltonians with potentially up to $\bigO(\nsys^4)$ terms and little structure, which made it challenging to match the complexity of methods based on plane waves and real-space grids. 
In this work, we show that a Trotter step for atomic orbitals can be implemented in depth $\bigO(\polylog(\nsys))$ without ancillas by combining a rigorous treatment of orbital localization, a hierarchical Hamiltonian decomposition based on the Fast Multipole Method, and shallow quantum Fourier arithmetic circuits.
By bounding the Trotter error, we obtain sublinear simulation depth, and our total gate count $\nsys^{5/3 + o(1)}$ matches the best scaling known for any basis.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

Simulating electrons in materials and molecules is among the most promising applications of digital quantum computing.
The performance of a quantum simulation algorithm is generally described with respect to three parameters: the evolution time $t$, the accuracy $\eps$, and a system-size parameter $\nsys$.
Most research on electronic structure simulation rests on one of two simulation paradigms: Trotter product formulas and the qubitization framework.
The performance in terms of $t$ and $\eps$ is understood well for both methods. 
For qubitization, the asymptotic scaling is $\bigO(t + \log\small(\eps^{-1}\small))$ \cite{low_hamiltonian_2019}, while the $p$th-order Trotter formula scales as $\bigO(t^{1 + 1/p}\eps^{-1/p})$ \cite{berry_efficient_2007}.
The scaling with $\nsys$, however, depends on the type of interactions and the decisions made in modeling the system.
Tight bounds are often not known, in particular for systems with less structured interactions.
Electronic structure simulation based on atomic orbitals is a primary example of this.
The classical computational framework of molecular electronic structure rests on atomic orbitals, which underpin many central concepts of chemistry, reflecting the insight that atoms remain meaningful subunits within a molecule.
Improving and understanding the system-size dependence is a long-standing problem in the field \cite{aspuru-guzik_simulated_2005,whitfield_simulation_2011,wecker_gate-count_2014,hastings_improving_2015,poulin_trotter_2015,mcclean_exploiting_2014,reiher_elucidating_2017,motta_low_2021,babbush_exponentially_2016,babbush_exponentially_2017,berry_qubitization_2019,von_burg_quantum_2021,lee_even_2021,rocca_reducing_2024,liu_block_2025,gunther_phase_2026,low_denser_2026}.
