%% ==== file: expanded.tex ====
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
	We study the problem of learning the dense Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev (SYK) Hamiltonian from copies
	of its Gibbs state. Existing algorithms for Hamiltonian learning typically rely on geometric
	locality or bounded interaction degree and therefore do not apply to SYK, where each quartic
	interaction overlaps with \(\Theta(n^3)\) others. We show that this obstruction can be
	overcome by exploiting the random mean-field structure of the model. \emph{At any constant
	temperature}, we prove that with high probability over the SYK couplings, the entire
	Hamiltonian can be learned to inverse-polynomial accuracy using polynomially many samples.
	Furthermore, when the inverse temperature is restricted to be a sufficiently
	small constant, we construct a quasipolynomial-time learning algorithm which is
	qualitatively different from the sample-efficient algorithm.

\end{abstract}

\newpage 
\setcounter{tocdepth}{2}
{\footnotesize \tableofcontents}

\newpage

\section{Introduction}

Understanding the complexity of quantum states has been a central focus of quantum computer science, with recent years bringing the new measure of \textit{learnability} to the picture. Rooted in the practical design of quantum computers as well as philosophical questions about the scope of knowledge that quantum mechanics allows, a wide range of quantum objects have been shown to be learnable in recent years (see~\cite{AnshuArunachalam24} for a survey). A notable class is that of \emph{quantum Gibbs states}, which form an expressive family of states and have been a subject of intense study in physics for over a century.   The problem of \textit{Hamiltonian learning} from Gibbs states is as follows. Can one reconstruct the Hamiltonian governing a quantum many-body system, described~as
$$
    H(\vec g)=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{m} g_\alpha E_\alpha
$$
for some known fixed basis $\{E_\alpha\}_\alpha$, given copies of the Gibbs state:
$$
    \gamma_{\vec g}
      =\frac{e^{-\beta H(\vec g)}}
             {\operatorname{tr}_{\rm ordinary}(e^{-\beta H(\vec g)})} \quad ?
$$
The goal is to recover the couplings $\vec g$ with prescribed error using as few copies of
$\gamma_{\vec g}$ and as little running time as possible. This is the quantum analogue of learning
an undirected \emph{graphical model} from samples.
Besides being a fundamental inverse
problem, Hamiltonian learning has promising applications in the calibration, verification of quantum simulators and the extraction of effective microscopic models from
thermal data.

One compelling setting for this inverse problem is provided by strongly interacting quantum many-body systems, where the  interactions in the Hamiltonian  
encode highly nontrivial correlations even though the description of the Hamiltonian is
specified by only polynomially many coupling parameters. Among the most prominent models of strongly interacting Hamiltonians is the well-known \emph{Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev} (SYK) model~\cite{SachdevYe93,Kitaev15,MaldacenaStanford16,MaldacenaShenkerStanford16, KKZ19}, which has become central to quantum chaos and strongly interacting fermions, as well as a benchmark
for the limits of classical simulation. In this work,  we initiate  the Hamiltonian learning problem for SYK models by asking
\begin{quote}
\begin{center}
\emph{Can a dense SYK Hamiltonian be learned in polynomial time,\\ given copies of its Gibbs state at constant temperature?}
\end{center}
\end{quote}
Two conceptual reasons motivate this question. 
First, a sequence of works initiated by~\cite{anshu2020sample} showed that geometrically local Hamiltonians can be learned with polynomial sample complexity. Subsequently~\cite{haah2022optimal}  obtained essentially optimal sample and time complexity in the high-temperature regime for a broader class of Hamiltonians. More recently~\cite{BLMT2024_learning,Narayanan25} gave a polynomial-time algorithm at every constant temperature, and then~\cite{CAN25} obtained further local-learning guarantees. Central to these results is some form of locality or bounded interaction degree.
The SYK model is the canonical testbed of whether this obstruction is fundamental. Formally, the SYK Hamiltonian is defined as follows: for even $q$
$$
    H_{\mathrm{SYK}}^{(q)}(\vec g)
      =\sigma_{n,q}\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq[n]\\ |S|=q}}
          g_S\,\Gamma_S^{(q)},\qquad
    \sigma_{n,q}=\sqrt{(q-1)!/n^{q-1}},\qquad
    \Gamma_S^{(q)}=-i^{q/2}\prod_{j\in S}\psi_j ,
$$
where the $\psi_i$ are Majorana operators satisfying $\{\psi_i,\psi_j\}=2\delta_{ij}\Id$ and
$\vec g$ is a realization of $\vec \bsg=(\bsg_S)_S$ with independent $\mc N(0,1)$ coordinates.
The overall phase is chosen so that at $q=4$,
$\Gamma_S^{(4)}=\Gamma_S=\prod_{j\in S}\psi_j$ and
$\sigma_{n,4}=\sigma_n=\sqrt{6/n^3}$. Each summand is $q$-local, but the interaction pattern is all-to-all.
The model combines several features that make the learning problem nontrivial: its terms strongly fail to commute, its Gibbs states are
genuinely non-Gaussian, and its physically relevant behavior occurs at constant inverse temperature. For quartic SYK,  every interaction overlaps
with $\Theta(n^3)$ other interactions. Consequently, tools such as Lieb-Robinson bounds used in \cite{anshu2020sample, BLMT2024_learning, CAN25} do not apply. The high-temperature condition in \cite{haah2022optimal} also depends on the degree, forcing
$\beta= n^{-\Omega(1)}$ which does not cover the  case of fixed inverse temperature $\beta>0$. 

Our second motivation is to test whether constructive learning results can be obtained for models that exhibit strong chaotic behavior. The dynamics generated by the SYK Hamiltonian is chaotic, and hence one may expect that it may exhibit pseudo-random behaviour. Learnability of the SYK Hamiltonian would offer a complementary viewpoint and possibly reveal new structures in the model.

\subsection{Main result}
Our first result shows that the dense interaction structure of SYK does not prevent sample-efficient Hamiltonian learning. For quartic SYK, at every fixed inverse temperature \(\beta>0\), the complete coupling vector can be recovered to inverse-polynomial accuracy from
\[
    \operatorname{poly}\!\left(n,1/\varepsilon,
        \log(1/\zeta)\right)
\]
many copies of the Gibbs state, with high probability over the random couplings and conditional success probability at least $1-\zeta$ over the measurement outcomes.
In particular, the sample complexity is polynomial in the parameters, despite the polynomial interaction degree. To our
knowledge, this is the first constant-temperature Hamiltonian-learning
guarantee for a dense, random, noncommuting mean-field~ensemble.

\paragraph{Sample-efficient learning.}
Our first theorem gives polynomial sample complexity at every fixed positive temperature. For technical convenience, throughout the paper we work with the normalized trace
\[
    \Tr(X):=\tr(X)/d_n,
    \qquad
    d_n:=2^{n/2},
\]
where \(d_n\) is the dimension of the Hilbert space of \(n\) Majorana
fermions.\footnote{Here, observe that every pair of Majorana modes forms one complex Fermionic mode, whose occupation number
is either \(0\) or \(1\), so \(n\) Majorana modes correspond to \(n/2\)
Fermionic modes and hence to a \(2^{n/2}\)-dimensional Hilbert space. Hence we assume $n$ is even throughout the paper.} Thus \(\Tr(I)=1\). 

\begin{restatable}[Sample-efficient learning at every fixed positive
	temperature]{theorem}{samplealltemp}
\label{sampleall:thm:learning}
Fix a known $\beta>0$, $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, and $\zeta\in(0,1/2)$. Then, for all sufficiently large $n$ (depending on $\beta$, $\varepsilon$, and $\zeta$), there is a procedure using
\begin{equation}\label{sampleall:eq:samplecomplexity}
 n^{O(1+\beta^2)}\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/\zeta)
\end{equation}
copies of the Gibbs state $d_n^{-1}\rho_\beta(\vec \bsg)$ with the following guarantee: with probability
at least $1-O_\beta(1/n)$ over the random disorder $\vec \bsg$, the procedure outputs an estimate
$\vec g_\mathrm{meas}$ satisfying
\[
    \|\vec g_\mathrm{meas}-\vec \bsg\|_2\leq \varepsilon
\]
with probability $\geq 1-\zeta$ over the measurement outcomes.
\end{restatable}

\begin{remark}[Even interaction order]
\label{rem:sample_even_q}
The conclusion of \Cref{sampleall:thm:learning} extends to $H_{\mathrm{SYK}}^{(q)}$
for every fixed even $q\geq2$ and known $\beta>0$. For sufficiently large even
$n\geq q$ depending on $\beta,q$, the sample bound becomes
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 r_{\beta,q}&=2q+2eq(2q+1)\beta(1+\beta),\\
 N&\leq C_{\beta,q}\left(n^{4r_{\beta,q}+q+1}
       +n^{2r_{\beta,q}+q+1}\varepsilon^{-2}\right)\log(n/\zeta),
 \end{aligned}
\]
with disorder success probability $1-O_{\beta,q}(n^{-1})$ and the same conditional
measurement guarantee and ranges of $\varepsilon,\zeta$.

Only the following changes to the proof are needed. Set $m=\binom nq$ and use
$\sigma_{n,q}^2=(q-1)!/n^{q-1}$. The coefficient filter in
\eqref{sampleall:eq:filter} averages over the $2^q$ subsets of a $q$-element support.
Using $(q-1)$-element sets in the anticommutation argument of
\Cref{alltemp:lem:elementary} gives
$\sigma_{n,q}\|\sum_Iu_I\Gamma_I^{(q)}\|_{\rm op}\leq\|\vec u\|_2/\sqrt q$;
thus the Hessian Lipschitz constant becomes $6\beta^3/q^{3/2}$.
In \Cref{alltemp:lem:moments}, a nonzero commutator increases the support by at most
$q-2$, so at most $qk\binom{n-1}{q-1}$ labels are available at each of the first $k$
steps. Since $\sigma_{n,q}^2\binom{n-1}{q-1}\leq1$, this yields
\[
 M_{2k}\leq[2qk(1+\beta)]^{2k},\qquad
 s_{\beta,q}=\frac1{2eq(1+\beta)}.
\]
Taking $p=1+s_{\beta,q}/\beta$, the same concentration, fractional-moment, and BKM
arguments give $\nabla^2\log Z\succeq c_{\beta,q}n^{-r_{\beta,q}}I$.
Finally, $m^2\sigma_{n,q}^2=O_q(n^{q+1})$ gives the stated sample bound.
The constants $C_{\beta,q},c_{\beta,q}>0$ depend only on $\beta,q$; at $q=4$ this
recovers the theorem above.
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Quasi-polynomial time learning.}
Our second result gives a quasipolynomial-time learning algorithm at
sufficiently high constant temperature and achieves small $\ell_2$ error in the couplings. 
For the running-time statement, we use the standard qubit representation of the Majoranas and  that $\beta$ is specified to
polynomially many bits of precision to the algorithm.

\begin{restatable}[Quasi-polynomial time learning]{theorem}{timelearning}
\label{thm:time_learning}
Fix a known  constant $0 < \beta \leq \beta_\mathrm{algorithm}$, a constant $0 < c < 1$, and
$\zeta \in (0,1)$. For all sufficiently large $n$, there is an algorithm which uses
\[
	N = \O_\beta\!\Paren{n^{13}\log(n/\zeta)}
\]
copies of the Gibbs state $d_n^{-1} \rho_\beta(\vec \bsg)$ with the following guarantee: with probability
at least $1-\O_\beta(n^{-2(1-c)})$ over the random disorder $\vec \bsg$, the algorithm outputs
$\vec g_\mathrm{meas}$ satisfying
\[
	\frac{1}{\sqrt{\binom{n}{4}}} \|\vec g_\mathrm{meas} - \vec \bsg\|_2 \leq n^{-c},
\]
with probability $\geq 1-\zeta$ over the measurements. The runtime is
\[
	n^{O(\log n)} + \widetilde O_\beta\!\left(n^{14}\log(n/\zeta)\right)\,.
\]
\end{restatable}

\paragraph{Temperature dependence.}
The sample-efficient guarantee holds for every fixed $\beta>0$. For the time-efficient
algorithm, fix an absolute constant $C_\star\geq1$ sufficiently large to dominate the
absolute majorant constants in the background and observable-diagram estimates of
\Cref{sec:degree_proof}, and set
\[
 \beta_\mathrm{algorithm}=\min\left\{
   \frac{1}{768MC_\star},
	\frac{\beta_\mathrm{thermal}}{8\sqrt{15}}\right\}\,,\qquad
 M=\max\{1,c^{(\mathrm{deg})}_1,c^{(\mathrm{deg})}_2\}.
\]

The first restriction comes from multiplying two factors. The first factor $\frac 1 {64C_\star}$ will
give us global control over convergence of various series that will arise when counting polymers via
Wick expansion towards the proof of \Cref{lem:degree_bound}. For the second factor, $c^{(\mathrm{deg})}_1$ and
$c^{(\mathrm{deg})}_2$ relate to the degree bounds of our estimator and the bound $1/(12M)$
will yield stability of our low-degree calibration subroutine. The second restriction $\beta_{\rm
thermal}/(8\sqrt{15})$ supplies the threshold for our improved zero-free result and bounds the error
for the truncation of our proxy for $\Tr[\Gamma_I \rho_\beta(\vec g)]$.

\subsection{Proof overview of sample-efficient learning}

We first give an overview of the algorithm establishing sample-efficient learnability of SYK
Hamiltonians. The overall strategy follows the maximum-entropy framework of~\cite{anshu2020sample}: learning the Hamiltonian from Gibbs states reduces to proving that the log-partition function is \emph{strongly convex}. The main obstacle is that the SYK Hamiltonian has all-to-all connectivity. Every quartic term intersects $\Theta(n^3)$ other terms, so arguments that lose polynomially in the interaction degree do not yield a nontrivial statement at constant temperature. Instead, we exploit  two  features
of SYK: the random mean-field structure of its couplings and the algebraic structure of the Majorana operators. 

\subsubsection{Maximum entropy and strong convexity}
\label{sec:maximumentropy}
Let $\calI=\binom{[n]}4$, $m=|\calI|$, and recall that
\[
 H(\vec \bsg)=\sigma_n\sum_{I\in\calI}\bsg_I\Gamma_I,
 \qquad
 \sigma_n=\sqrt{6/n^3},
 \qquad
 \bsg_I\stackrel{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mc N(0,1),
 \qquad
 \rho_\beta(\vec \bsg)=\frac{e^{-\beta H(\vec \bsg)}}{Z(\beta,\vec \bsg)}.
\]
We begin by recalling the maximum-entropy reduction of \cite{anshu2020sample}. First, one can observe that the quartic expectation values
\[
    \mu_{\beta,I}(\vec \bsg)
    :=
    \Tr\!\left[\rho_\beta(\vec \bsg)\Gamma_I\right],
    \qquad I\in\mathcal I_4,
\]
form a \emph{sufficient statistic} for the Gibbs family, i.e., the collection
$\{\mu_{\beta,I}(\vec \bsg)\}_{I\in\mathcal I_4}$ \emph{uniquely} determines
the  coupling vector $\vec \bsg$.  Consequently, if the exact expectation vector
$\vec \mu_\beta=(\mu_{\beta,I}(\vec \bsg))_{I\in\calI}$ were known exactly, then $\vec h = \vec \bsg$ would be the unique minimizer of the optimization program
\[
 \mc L(\vec h)
 =
 \Phi(\vec h)+\beta\sigma_n\,\vec h\cdot\vec \mu_\beta,
 \qquad
 \Phi(\vec h)=\log Z(\beta,\vec h).
\]
Indeed, $\nabla\Phi(\vec \bsg) = -\beta\sigma_n \vec \mu_\beta$, and hence $\nabla \mc
L(\vec \bsg)=0$. Of course, we only have empirical estimates
$\vec \mu_{\beta,\mathrm{meas}}$. We therefore minimize
\[
 \mc L_\mathrm{meas}(\vec h)
 =
 \Phi(\vec h)+\beta\sigma_n\,\vec h\cdot\vec\mu_{\beta,\mathrm{meas}}
\]
over a known compact convex set containing $\vec \bsg$.  Thus the optimization problem above reduces to a stability question: how far
can the minimizer move when the linear term in the objective is 
perturbed? Strong convexity of the function $\Phi$ around the true parameter
$\vec \bsg$ gives precisely the required control to convert an
$\ell_2$ error in the measured expectations into an $\ell_2$ error in
the recovered couplings. Suppose
\begin{align}
\label{eq:strongconvexity}
 \nabla^2\Phi(\vec \bsg)\succeq \lambda_n I
\end{align}
for some $\lambda_n>0$. Then $\mc L_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is stable under perturbations of the measured
expectation values, with a bound depending on $\lambda_n$. Ideally, one would like to prove a uniform lower bound on
$\nabla^2\Phi(\vec g)$ throughout the feasible region. In our setting,
however, we are only able to establish such a bound at the random target
$\vec \bsg$ itself. We show that this is nevertheless sufficient. In
particular, \Cref{alltemp:lem:hessian-lipschitz} shows that the Hessian is
Lipschitz:
\[
	\|\nabla^2\Phi(\vec h)-\nabla^2\Phi(\vec h')\|_{\rm op} \leq \poly(\beta)\cdot \|\vec h-\vec h'\|_2,
\]
Consequently, if Eq.~\eqref{eq:strongconvexity} holds, then  $\Phi$ remains $(\lambda_n/2)$-strongly convex in a ball of radius
$\lambda_n/\poly(\beta)$ around $\vec \bsg$. A standard boundary argument then can be used to show that if
\[
 \|\vec\mu_{\beta,\mathrm{meas}}-\vec \mu_\beta\|_2
 \leq
 \min\Brac{\frac{\lambda_n\varepsilon}{8\beta\sigma_n}, \frac{\lambda_n^2}{16\beta\sigma_n \poly(\beta)}}\,,
\]
then every minimizer $\vec g_\mathrm{meas}$ of $\mc L_\mathrm{meas}$ satisfies
$ \|\vec g_\mathrm{meas}-\vec \bsg\|_2\leq\varepsilon.$
Since each $\Gamma_I$ is a $\{\pm1\}$-valued observable, inverse-polynomial accuracy in the moments requires only polynomially many samples. Thus the problem reduces to proving, with high probability over the SYK disorder,
\[
 \nabla^2\Phi(\vec \bsg)\succeq n^{-O_\beta(1)}I.
\]

\subsubsection{From the Hessian to an ordinary variance}
We next reduce strong convexity of the log-partition function to a lower bound on  
thermal variance.  Fix a direction $\vec u\in\R^m$ and associate to it the quartic observable
$    A_{\vec u}:=\sum_{I\in\calI}u_I\Gamma_I.$ 
The Hessian of the log-partition function in the direction $\vec u$ has a particularly clean
interpretation.  Differentiating
$\Phi(\vec g)=\log Z(\beta,\vec g)$ twice gives
\begin{align}
\label{eq:variancebound}
    \vec u^\top\nabla^2\Phi(\vec g)\vec u
    =
    \beta^2\sigma_n^2
    \Var^{\BKM}_{\rho_\beta(\vec g)}(A_{\vec u}),
\end{align}
where the Bogoliubov--Kubo--Mori variance is
\begin{align}
\label{eq:bkmvariance}
    \Var^{\BKM}_{\rho}(A)
    :=
    \int_0^1
    \Tr\!\left[
        \rho^s A_0 \rho^{1-s}A_0
    \right]ds,
    \qquad
    A_0:=A-\Tr[\rho A]I.
\end{align}
This is the non-commutative analogue of the fact that the Hessian of a classical log-partition function is a covariance matrix.
The only difference is
that, because $A_{\vec u}$ need not commute with $\rho_\beta$, the usual variance is replaced by
the BKM variance. It is useful, however, to work with the ordinary variance
\begin{align}
\label{eq:usualvariance}
    \Var_{\rho}(A)
    =
    \Tr[\rho A_0^2] 
\end{align}
and below we relate \Cref{eq:bkmvariance} and \Cref{eq:usualvariance}. Diagonalizing
$H(\vec g)$, and writing $q_a=e^{-\beta\lambda_a}/(d_nZ(\beta,\vec g))$ for the Gibbs weights, one can express these terms as
\[
    \Var^{\BKM}_{\rho_\beta}(A)
    =
    \sum_{a,b}\,|(A_0)_{ab}|^2\cdot \int_0^1 q_a^s q_b^{1-s}\,ds,
    \qquad
    \Var_{\rho_\beta}(A)
    =
    \sum_{a,b}q_a\,|(A_0)_{ab}|^2.
\]
Now, letting
$\Delta_{\vec g}=\lambda_{\max}(H(\vec g))-\lambda_{\min}(H(\vec g))$
denote the spectral diameter, observe that 
$$
 \int_0^1 q_a^s q_b^{1-s}\,ds\geq \frac{q_a}{1+\beta\Delta_{\vec g}},
 $$
hence
\begin{align}
\label{eq:BKMtoclassical}
    \Var^{\BKM}_{\rho_\beta(\vec g)}(A)
    \geq
    \frac{1}{1+\beta\Delta_{\vec g}}
    \Var_{\rho_\beta(\vec g)}(A) \stackrel{\eqref{eq:variancebound}}{\implies}
    \vec u^\top\nabla^2\Phi(\vec g)\vec u
    \geq
    \frac{\beta^2\sigma_n^2}
         {1+\beta\Delta_{\vec g}}
    \Var_{\rho_\beta(\vec g)}(A_{\vec u}).
\end{align}
For a typical SYK instance, $\|H(\vec g)\|_{\op}=O(n)$, and hence
$\Delta_{\vec g}=O(n)$.  Thus the passage from the Hessian to ordinary variance loses only a
polynomial factor.  In particular, it is sufficient to establish
\[
    \Var_{\rho_\beta(\vec g)}(A_{\vec u})
    \geq
    n^{-O_\beta(1)}\|\vec u\|_2^2
\]
 for every direction $\vec u$.
The remaining task is therefore purely a variance lower bound.  

\subsubsection{Exact coefficient extraction and local perturbations}

It remains to prove an inverse-polynomial lower bound on 
$\Var_{\rho_\beta}(A_{\vec u})$.  Normalize $\|\vec u\|_2=1$ and~let
\[
    V=A_{\vec u}=\sum_{I\in\calI}u_I\Gamma_I,
    \qquad
    V_0=V-\Tr(\rho_\beta V)\Id.
\]
Our first observation is that, from an arbitrary global quartic observable $V$, we can
isolate any one of its coefficients \emph{exactly}, without paying any factor depending on the
interaction degree. Let $S \in \calI$. Define the Majorana twirl,
\[
	\mc P_S(X) = \frac 1 {16} \sum_{A \subseteq S} (-1)^{|A|} \Gamma_A X \Gamma_A^\dagger\,,
\]
which isolates the coefficient $u_S$. Using $\Gamma_A\Gamma_I\Gamma_A^\dagger = (-1)^{|A\cap I|}\Gamma_I,$ we have that
\begin{align}
\label{eq:termextraction}
	\mc P_S(V_0) = \frac 1 {16} \sum_{A\subseteq S} (-1)^{|A|} \Gamma_A V_0 \Gamma_A^\dagger =
	\frac 1 {16} \sum_{I \in \calI} u_I \Paren{ \sum_{A\subseteq S} (-1)^{|A|+|A\cap I|}
	}\Gamma_I = u_S\Gamma_S\,
\end{align}
where we used that the inner sum vanishes unless $I=S$. Thus one coefficient of an arbitrary quartic observable can be extracted exactly, with no dependence
on the interaction degree. After algebraic manipulation, this isolation procedure allows us to write
\[
	u_S^2 \leq \frac 1 {16} \sum_{A \subseteq S} \Tr[\rho_A V_0^2]\,,\qquad \rho_A = U_A \rho
	U_A^\dagger\,
\]
where $U_A=\Gamma_A$. 
Thus, we have reduced the problem to relating the variance of the locally perturbed Gibbs state
$\rho_A$ to that of the true state $\rho$. The comparison is controlled by a Petz R\'enyi power
\cite{petz1986quasi} between the two states,
\[
	R_{p,A} = \frac{\Tr[e^{-(\beta+s) H} e^{s U_A H U_A^\dagger}]}{Z(\beta, \vec g)} =
	\frac{Z_A(\beta, s, \vec g)}{Z(\beta, \vec g)}\,.
\]
This argument is made in \Cref{sampleall:lem:variance}. Next, we show in \Cref{alltemp:thm:quench} that the corresponding annealed quantity satisfies
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:annealed_ratio}
	\E_{\vec \bsg} Z_A(\beta, s, \vec \bsg) / \E_{\vec \bsg} Z(\beta, \vec \bsg) \leq \frac 8
	3\,.
\end{equation}
Assuming this bound, we restrict to the event
$Z(\beta,\vec \bsg)\geq n^{-1}\E_{\vec \bsg}Z(\beta,\vec \bsg)$, which has high probability.
On this event, the denominator can be replaced by its annealed value at a polynomial cost;
Markov's inequality then bounds the average of the ratios $R_{p,A}$ with high probability.
Finally, this yields the chain of inequalities,
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:variance_lower}
	\Var_{\rho_\beta}(V) \geq \Paren{ \binom n 3 m^{p-1} \frac 1 {16} \sum_{|S| = 4} \sum_{A
	\subseteq S} R_{p, A}}^{-1/(p-1)} \|\vec u\|_2^2 \geq \Paren{n^{4p+5}}^{-1/(p-1)} \|\vec u\|_2^2 \geq
	n^{-4 - 9\beta / s} \|\vec u\|_2^2\,,
\end{equation}
where we have taken $p = 1 + s / \beta$. 

\paragraph{Proving \Cref{eq:annealed_ratio}.} We want to control the degree to which a local
operation $\Gamma_A$ can affect the Gibbs state, as measured by the Petz R\'enyi power,
\[
	\Tr[(U_A \rho U_A^\dagger)^p \rho^{1 - p}]\,.
\]
This bound is reminiscent of the ``leakage'' controlled in \cite{arad2016connecting}, and indeed,
bounding such a quantity directly yields a sample-efficient algorithm for bounded-degree graphs
(see \cite{anshu2020sample} and a simplified proof in \Cref{app:bounded_degree}). In an earlier
version of this work, we controlled this quantity by Taylor expanding exponentials $e^{-\beta H}$
with respect to $\beta$ and applying Koteck\'y--Preiss, as in our time-efficient result. However,
generative AI observed that we can instead bound the annealed local-quench ratio by a series of
iterated commutator moments. Writing $H=H(\vec \bsg)$ and $C_k=C_k(\vec \bsg)$ inside expectations,
the terms are, for $k\geq0$,
\[
	\Paren{\frac {s^{2k}}{(2k)!}} M_{2k} = \Paren{\frac {s^{2k}}{(2k)!}}\frac{\E_{\vec \bsg}
	\Tr[e^{-\beta H} C_k C_k^\dagger]}{\E_{\vec \bsg} Z(\beta, \vec \bsg)}\,, \qquad C_k(\vec g) =
	\operatorname{ad}_{H(\vec g)}^k (U_A)\,.
\]
Expanding the commutators and counting the terms which survive when we average over the
SYK couplings yields the bound $M_{2k} \leq [8k ( 1 + \beta)]^{2k}$ in \Cref{alltemp:lem:moments}.
Choosing $s=O((1+\beta)^{-1})$ makes the resulting series summable and yields
\Cref{eq:annealed_ratio}.

\subsubsection{Completing the analysis}
Putting together \Cref{eq:variancebound}, \Cref{eq:BKMtoclassical}, \Cref{eq:variance_lower}, we get
that
\[
	\nabla^2\Phi(\vec \bsg)\succeq\lambda_n\Id, \qquad \lambda_n = \frac{\beta^2 \sigma_n^2}{1 +
	\beta\Delta_{\vec \bsg}} n^{-O_\beta(1)} = n^{-O_\beta(1)}.
\]
Since each $\Gamma_I$ is a
$\{\pm1\}$-valued observable, its expectation can be estimated from repeated measurements
using Hoeffding's inequality.  Estimating every $\mu_{\beta,I}$ to accuracy
$\delta/\sqrt m$ and taking a union bound over all $I$ gives
$\|\vec \mu_{\beta, \mathrm{meas}}-\vec \mu_\beta\|_2\leq\delta$ using
$\textsf{poly}(n,1/\delta)\log(1/\zeta)$ copies.   As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:maximumentropy} this implies
\[
\|\vec g_{\mathrm{meas}}-\vec \bsg\|_2\leq\varepsilon.
\]
with probability at least $1-\zeta$ over the measurements.    Thus, despite the all-to-all interaction structure of SYK, inverse-polynomial accuracy in the couplings can be achieved with only polynomially many copies of the Gibbs state, proving our first result. 

\subsection{Time-efficient learning}
\label{sec:intro-time-efficient}

In the previous section, our main result was an \emph{information-theoretic} result that SYK models are learnable given copies of the Gibbs state. However, the main drawback was that the empirical maximum-entropy principle need not be  solvable in polynomial time. Recall that the sample-efficient algorithm above is based on solving the following optimization problem
\[
    \mathcal L(\vec h)
    =
    \log Z(\beta,\vec h)
    +
    \beta\sigma_n\,\vec h\cdot\vec\mu_\beta,
\]
whose unique minimizer is the \emph{true coupling} vector $\vec g$.  While this
gives an information-theoretically efficient reconstruction procedure, it
does not immediately yield an efficient algorithm for learning the unknown SYK~Hamiltonian.

\subsubsection{First-order inversion}
Unlike the sample-efficient procedure, the time-efficient algorithm does not
solve the maximum-entropy optimization problem.  
Instead, it works with the same measured quartic expectations and seeks to directly invert the
map from the SYK couplings to these observables.
 Recall that
$    H(\vec g)
    =
    \sigma_n\sum_{I\in\mathcal I_4} g_I\Gamma_I,$ 
where $   \sigma_n=\sqrt{{6}/{n^3}}
$. 
Define
\[
    \mu_{\beta,I}(\vec g)
    :=
    \operatorname{Tr}[\rho_\beta(\vec g)\Gamma_I].
\]
At high temperature, these expectations are approximately proportional to
the corresponding couplings.  Indeed, a first-order Taylor expansion of the
Gibbs state around $\beta=0$ gives
\[
    \mu_{\beta,I}(\vec g)
    =
    -\beta\,\operatorname{Tr}[\Gamma_I H(\vec g)]
    +O(\beta^2)
    =
    -\beta\sigma_n g_I+O(\beta^2),
\]
where in the last equality we used the orthogonality relations of the
Majorana operators,
$\operatorname{Tr}[\Gamma_I\Gamma_J]=\delta_{I,J}$.
To recover $g_I$ at first order, we normalize the thermal expectations by $-\beta\sigma_n$, defining
\[
    U_{\beta,I}(\vec g) := -\frac{\mu_{\beta,I}(\vec g)}{\beta\sigma_n} = - \frac{\Tr[\Gamma_I
    \rho_\beta(\vec g)]} {\beta\sigma_n}.
\]
With this normalization, the thermal expectation map is close to the
identity.  More precisely, expanding $\mu_{\beta,I}$ one order further gives
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:intro-time-expansion}
    U_{\beta,I}(\vec g)
    =
    g_I-\frac{\beta\sigma_n}{2}
    \sum_{J_1\triangle J_2=I}
    \chi(I;J_1,J_2)\,g_{J_1}g_{J_2}
    +O(\beta^2),
\end{equation}
where
\[
    \chi(I;J_1,J_2)
    :=
    \operatorname{sign}
    \Tr[\Gamma_I\Gamma_{J_1}\Gamma_{J_2}].
\]
Thus, after the natural rescaling by $\beta\sigma_n$, the measured expectations agree with the
disorder vector $\vec g$ at linear order, and the remaining task is to correct the nonlinear terms
beginning with the quadratic contribution in \Cref{eq:intro-time-expansion}. This observation almost
gives an algorithm by itself, but not quite.  For a fixed $I$, the quadratic term in
\Cref{eq:intro-time-expansion} contains $N_2=\Theta(n^2)$ essentially orthogonal Gaussian monomials.
Since $\sigma_n=\Theta(n^{-3/2})$ and there are $N_2=\Theta(n^2)$ orthogonal quadratic monomials,
the Gaussian $L^2$ norm of this quadratic correction is
\[
    \Theta_\beta(\sigma_n\sqrt{N_2})
    =
    \Theta_\beta(n^{-1/2}).
\]
Thus, even if one were given the thermal expectations exactly, the naive inversion map 
leaves an $n^{-1/2}$-scale quadratic bias in each coordinate.  The main
challenge in the time-efficient argument which we deal with below is to identify and
cancel this leading nonlinear contribution.

\subsubsection{A polynomial approximation to $U_\beta$}
\label{sec:poly_approximation}
The exact map $\vec U_\beta=(U_{\beta,I}(\vec g))_I$ is still difficult to analyze directly because
it contains the random partition function in the denominator, i.e., 
\[
    U_{\beta,I}(\vec g)
    =
    -
    \frac{
        \operatorname{Tr}[
            \Gamma_Ie^{-\beta H(\vec g)}
        ]
    }{
        \beta\sigma_n Z(\beta,\vec g)
    }.
\]
So, we first approximate this map by an explicit low-degree polynomial in the Gaussian
disorder variables.~Write
\[
    Z(\beta,\vec g)
    =
    Z_{\rm ann}(\beta)
    \bigl(1+\Delta_\beta(\vec g)\bigr),
    \qquad
    Z_{\rm ann}(\beta)
    :=
    \E_{\vec \bsg}[Z(\beta,\vec \bsg)].
\]
Applying the Taylor expansion
$    \frac{1}{1+\Delta_\beta}
    =
    1-\Delta_\beta
    +
    O(\Delta_\beta^2)$ 
suggests replacing the factor $(1+\Delta_\beta)^{-1}$ by its first-order approximation. 
This leads to the untruncated proxy
\[
    V_{\beta,I}^{\mathrm{full}}(\vec g)
    :=
    -
    \frac{
        \operatorname{Tr}[
            \Gamma_Ie^{-\beta H(\vec g)}
        ]
    }{
        \beta\sigma_n Z_{\rm ann}(\beta)
    }
    \left(
        2-
        \frac{Z(\beta,\vec g)}{Z_{\rm ann}(\beta)}
    \right).
\]
We then truncate its Taylor series in $\beta$ at degree
$K=O(\log n)$. Since the coefficient of $\beta^k$ is a polynomial of degree $O(k)$ in
$\vec g$, the resulting proxy $V_{\beta,I}$ is a Gaussian polynomial of
degree $O(\log n)$. There are a couple of subtleties in implementing this idea. 

\begin{enumerate}
    \item First, replacing
$(1+\Delta_\beta)^{-1}$ by $1-\Delta_\beta$ produces an error quadratic
in $\Delta_\beta$.  The previously known second-moment estimate~\cite{zlokapa2026rigorous},
\[
    \E_{\vec \bsg}|\Delta_\beta(\vec \bsg)|^2
    =
    O(n^{-1}),
\]
is sufficient to control this quadratic error in $L_1$, but our final
reconstruction uses quadratic combinations of the approximations
$V_{\beta,I}$ to the rescaled expectations $U_{\beta,I}$ and measures the
resulting error in $L^2$.  Concretely, we must control terms of the form
\[
    \bigl\|
        (U_{\beta,J}-V_{\beta,J})\,U_{\beta,K}
    \bigr\|_{L^2}
    \le
    \|U_{\beta,J}-V_{\beta,J}\|_{L^4}
    \|U_{\beta,K}\|_{L^4},
\]
by H\"older's inequality.  Thus we need $L^4$ control of
$U_{\beta,I}-V_{\beta,I}$, rather than only control in expectation.
Moreover, the error incurred by replacing $(1+\Delta_\beta)^{-1}$ by
$1-\Delta_\beta$ contributes a term of the form
$\Delta_\beta^2 U_{\beta,I}$, so controlling the proxy error in $L^4$
requires fixed higher moments of $\Delta_\beta$.  We therefore prove the
stronger weighted estimate
\begin{equation}
    \|\Delta_\beta\|_{2,s}
    \le
    C_s n^{-1},
    \label{eq:intro-strong-thermal}
\end{equation}
for every fixed $s\ge1$.  For the algorithm it suffices to take
$s=\sqrt{15}$, since Gaussian hypercontractivity then controls all
$L^p$ norms up to $p=16$.  This strengthened estimate is one of
the main structural results specific to the time-efficient algorithm, and its
proof requires a more refined analysis of the Wick expansion
and associated polymer expansion than is needed for the
sample-efficient result.

\item Second, we truncate the $\beta$-expansion defining $V_{\beta,I}^{\mathrm{full}}$.
Define
\[
    V_{\beta,I}^{\mathrm{full}}(\vec g)
    =
    \sum_{k\ge 0} v_{I,k}(\vec g)\,\beta^k,
\text{ and }    V_{\beta,I}(\vec g)
    :=
    \sum_{k=0}^{K} v_{I,k}(\vec g)\,\beta^k.
\]
The nontrivial technical step is to obtain a uniform $L^4$ bound on $V_{z,I}^{\rm full}$ throughout a
constant complex neighborhood of the origin.  This follows from the strengthened estimates above,
together with zero-freeness of $Z_{\rm ann}(z)$.  Once this is established, Cauchy's estimate
bounding the derivatives of analytic functions gives
\[
    \|v_{I,k}\|_{L^4} \leq C\,[\beta_{\rm thermal}(\sqrt{15})]^{-k}\,.
\]
In the temperature regime of the algorithm, $|\beta|/\beta_{\rm thermal}(\sqrt{15})\le 1/8$, and hence
\[
    \|V_{\beta,I}^{\mathrm{full}} - V_{\beta,I}\|_{L^4} \leq C\sum_{k > K}8^{-k}.
\]
Taking $K = \Theta(\log n)$ makes this tail inverse-polynomially small; with the choice used in the
proof it is $O(n^{-3})$.  Combining this truncation error with the error from replacing $(1 +
\Delta_\beta)^{-1}$ by $1 - \Delta_\beta$ yields
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:intro-proxy-error}
    \max_{I\in\mathcal I_4} \|U_{\beta,I}-V_{\beta,I}\|_{L^4} \leq O_\beta(n^{-3/2}).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}  

\subsubsection{Approximating the inverse map}
Now that we have an explicit polynomial approximation
$\vec V_\beta(\vec g)$ to the rescaled thermal expectations, the remaining
task is to approximately invert the map
$    \vec g \longmapsto \vec V_\beta(\vec g).$  A priori, even correcting only the quadratic part of this map seems
cumbersome: a general quadratic map
$\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m$ is specified by $\Theta(m^3)$ coefficients,
so directly learning or inverting its quadratic correction would require
handling a very large parameter space. 
The key simplification is that the SYK model has a large symmetry group,
which severely restricts the possible low-degree corrections.

The polynomial map $\vec V_\beta$ is covariant under sign changes of the
underlying Majorana modes and under permutations of the $n$ physical
indices.  To see why this is restrictive, consider a fixed output
coordinate $I$.  Under a sign change
$\vec x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{\pm1\}^n$, the coupling $g_J$ transforms as
\[
    g_J \longmapsto x_J g_J,
    \qquad
    x_J:=\prod_{j\in J}x_j,
\]
while the $I$-th output must transform as
\[
    V_{\beta,I}(\vec x\cdot\vec g)
    =
    x_I V_{\beta,I}(\vec g).
\]
This already rules out almost all degree-$\le2$ monomials.  A linear
monomial $g_J$ has the required sign only when $J=I$, while a quadratic
monomial $g_{J_1}g_{J_2}$ has the required sign only when
\[
    x_{J_1}x_{J_2}=x_I
    \qquad\text{for every }\vec x,
\]
which is equivalent to
$    J_1\triangle J_2=I.$ 
Thus, for a fixed output coordinate $I$, the only possible degree-one term
is $g_I$, and the only possible degree-two terms are precisely those
indexed by pairs $(J_1,J_2)$ satisfying
$J_1\triangle J_2=I$.

Permutation covariance then forces all such surviving terms to appear with
the same coefficient, up to the fermionic sign coming from the Majorana
ordering.  Consequently, the entire covariant Hermite degree-$\le2$ space
is spanned by only two vector-valued polynomials,
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:two_hermite_span}
	\vec\Phi_1(\vec g) = \vec g \text{ and } \Phi_{2,I}(\vec g) := \frac{1}{2\sqrt{N_2}}
	\sum_{J_1\triangle J_2=I} \chi(I;J_1,J_2)\, g_{J_1}g_{J_2}\,,
\end{equation}
where $\chi(I; J_1, J_2) = \mathsf{sign}(\Tr[\Gamma_I \Gamma_{J_1} \Gamma_{J_2}])$. Hence,
although the ambient quadratic space is enormous, the symmetries reduce the low-degree correction
problem to a two-dimensional one.
In particular, the quadratic statistic $\Phi_2$ is precisely the structure
of the leading correction appearing in
\Cref{eq:intro-time-expansion}.  This symmetry reduction is what makes it
possible to cancel the nonlinear bias without learning a large collection
of additional parameters. We therefore consider a reconstruction algorithm of the form
\begin{align}
\label{eq:calibcoeff}
    \vec f_{\rm reconstruct}(\vec x)
    =
    c_1\vec\Phi_1(\vec x)
    +
    c_2\vec\Phi_2(\vec x).
\end{align}
Rather than requiring
$\vec f_{\rm reconstruct}(\vec V_\beta(\vec g))=\vec g$ exactly, we only ask
that this identity hold in Hermite degrees at most two:
\begin{equation}
    \Pi_{\le2}
    \vec f_{\rm reconstruct}(\vec V_\beta(\vec g))
    =
    \vec g.
    \label{eq:intro-calibration-goal}
\end{equation}
By the covariance properties above, composition with $\vec V_\beta$ and
projection onto degree at most two defines a map from
$\operatorname{span}\{\Phi_1,\Phi_2\}$
to itself.
Hence \eqref{eq:intro-calibration-goal} reduces to inverting the
$2\times2$ matrix
\[
	M_\beta=M_\mathrm{cal}(\beta)=\begin{bmatrix} m_{1,1} & m_{1,2} \\ m_{2,1} & m_{2,2} \end{bmatrix}\quad \text{where}
	\quad m_{i,j}=\E_{\vec \bsg}[\Phi_{i,I}(\vec \bsg)\Phi_{j,I}(\vec{V}_\beta(\vec \bsg))]
	\quad\text{for any fixed }I\in\mc I_4,
\]
where we have appealed to the coordinatewise orthonormality of $\vec{\Phi}_i$. 
Therefore, choosing $c_1,c_2$ so that the degree-$\le2$ part of the
composition equals $\vec\Phi_1(\vec g)=\vec g$ amounts to solving the
$2\times2$ linear system 
\[
	\begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2\end{bmatrix} = M_\beta^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\
	0\end{bmatrix}\,.
\]
At infinite temperature, $\vec V_0(\vec g)=\vec g$, so $M_0=I$. Since it is analytic in $\beta$, that implies that, for sufficiently small constant $\beta$, $M_\beta$ remains close to the identity and is therefore
 invertible. Thus the coefficients $c_1,c_2$ can be chosen to
recover the linear term exactly and cancel the entire quadratic quantity.

\subsubsection{Why cancelling degree two is enough}
Recall that the two-dimensional reduction applies only to the Hermite degree-$\le 2$ part of the
map.  The full polynomial $\vec V_\beta(\vec g)$ still contains higher-degree terms:
\[
    \vec V_\beta(\vec g) =
    \underbrace{\Pi_{\le 2}\vec V_\beta(\vec g)}_{\text{two-dimensional by symmetry}} +
    \underbrace{\sum_{d\ge 3}\Pi_d\vec V_\beta(\vec g)}_{\text{higher-degree terms}}.
\]
The symmetry argument shows that the first part lies in $\operatorname{span}\{\Phi_1,\Phi_2\}$. By our choice of $c_1,c_2$ in \Cref{eq:calibcoeff},
$\vec f_{\rm reconstruct}$ recovers the linear term exactly and cancels the entire quadratic contribution.

The remaining issue is to show that these higher-degree terms are small.
A second technical ingredient is therefore a quantitative bound on the
higher-degree terms of $\vec V_\beta$. To this end,  we prove
\[
    \|\Pi_d\Phi_{1,I}(\vec V_\beta)\|_{L^2}
    \le
    c_d\,n^{-(d-1)/2},
    \qquad
    \|\Pi_d\Phi_{2,I}(\vec V_\beta)\|_{L^2}
    \le
    c_d\,n^{-(d-2)/2},
\]
where $c_d$ grows only exponentially in $d\log d$.  Since the quadratic
coefficient satisfies $|c_2|=O(n^{-1/2})$, the two linear and quadratic terms contribute on the
same scale, and the degree-$d$ part of the reconstructed error is
essentially
\[
    n^{-(d-1)/2}.
\]
Hence the degree-two contribution, which would be of order $n^{-1/2}$, is
precisely the obstruction that must be removed.  Once it is cancelled, the
first surviving term has degree three and is already of order $n^{-1}$.
Furthermore, since $\vec V_\beta$ has degree only $K=O(\log n)$, the remaining
Hermite tail is a finite rapidly decreasing sum, dominated by its
degree-three contribution.

Finally, the algorithm is given the true rescaled expectations
$\vec U_\beta$, rather than the polynomial approximation $\vec V_\beta$.
Since $\vec f_{\rm reconstruct}$ is quadratic, a direct application of
H\"older's inequality gives a Lipschitz-type bound in terms of
coordinatewise $L^4$ norms.  Combining this stability with
\Cref{eq:intro-proxy-error} transfers the error bound from
$\vec f_{\rm reconstruct}(\vec V_\beta)$ to
$\vec f_{\rm reconstruct}(\vec U_\beta)$ to get
\[
    \frac{1}{\sqrt m}
    \left\|
        \vec \bsg
        -
        \vec f_{\rm reconstruct}(\vec U_\beta)
    \right\|_{L^2}
    \le
    O_\beta(n^{-1}).
\]
Equivalently, for the normalized Hamiltonian parameters $    \vec\theta
    =
    \beta\sigma_n\vec \bsg,$
the estimator
\[
    \vec\theta_{\rm ideal}
    =
    \beta\sigma_n
    \vec f_{\rm reconstruct}(\vec U_\beta)
\]
satisfies
\[
    \frac{1}{\sqrt n}
    \|\vec\theta_{\rm ideal}-\vec\theta\|_{L^2}
    \le
    O_\beta(n^{-1}).
\]
\subsubsection{Overall running time}
It remains to account for the computational cost of the reconstruction. The coefficients $c_1,c_2$
depend only on $n$ and $\beta$, and not on the particular SYK instance, so they may be computed in a
preprocessing step from the truncated polynomial $V_\beta$.  Since the truncation degree is
$K=O(\log n)$, this preprocessing takes time
\[
    n^{O(K)} = 2^{\operatorname{polylog}(n)}\,.
\]
Once $c_1,c_2$ are fixed, evaluating
\[
    \vec g_{\rm meas} = \vec f_{\rm reconstruct}(\vec U_{\beta,\rm meas})
\]
is polynomial-time: for each $I \in \calI$, the quadratic term $\Phi_{2,I}$ contains only $N_2 =
\Theta(n^2)$ summands, and there are $m = \Theta(n^4)$ output coordinates.  Thus the reconstruction
itself can be implemented using $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ arithmetic operations. 

\section{Discussion}

Our work continues a line of papers which develop rigorous algorithms for the SYK model, including
\cite{hastings2022optimizing, basso2024optimizing} and, most recently,
\cite{zlokapa2026rigorous}. The first gives polynomial-time classical certificates and quantum
constant-factor approximations to the optimal energy of quartic SYK, while the second gives
dissipative algorithms with guarantees on the disorder-averaged energy for random local
Hamiltonians, including SYK. The work of \cite{zlokapa2026rigorous} instead estimates thermal
expectations at high temperature in quasi-polynomial classical time. These works develop rigorous
alternatives to heuristics such as the replica method, using different aspects of the random
Hamiltonian. In particular, the Wick-pair expansion of \cite{zlokapa2026rigorous}, which we extend
in our quasi-polynomial time algorithm, exploits Gaussian disorder to control higher-degree
contributions after disorder averaging. We expect that these techniques will lead to increasingly
effective algorithms for simulating, learning, and preparing low-energy states of the SYK model.

Classically, a closely related line of work
~\cite{anari2024universality,gaitonde2024unified,chandrasekaran2025learning} has established
increasingly powerful guarantees for learning the \emph{Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model}, a
widely studied model for disordered magnets. In this model, the Hamiltonian is classical and
2-local, given by $H(x)\triangleq \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i<j} g_{ij}x_ix_j$ for $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$
and $g_{ij}$ sampled i.i.d. from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. This model exhibits a replica symmetry breaking
phase transition at inverse temperature $\beta = 1$. The most recent work in this
line~\cite{chandrasekaran2025learning} established that one can learn the couplings $(g_{ij})$ given
samples from the Gibbs measure $\propto e^{-\beta H}$ even at $\beta = O(\sqrt{\log n})$, well
beyond this phase transition. Our result is qualitatively different in part because it is
conjectured that the SYK model does not exhibit such a phase transition. Our algorithm does however
bear resemblance to prior structural observations about the SK model below the phase transition:
in~\cite{el2024bounds,brennecke2024two}, bounds on the two-point correlation matrix for the SK model
below the phase transition were proven by relating that matrix to the disorder matrix itself. This
is the same premise behind our time-efficient algorithm, although we need to take higher-order local
observables than merely the sufficient statistics of the model.

\paragraph{The context of our results.} Our sample-efficient result begins by following the proof strategy developed by
\cite{anshu2020sample}; to prove sample-efficient learning, it suffices to show that the log
partition function is strongly convex. In the classical setting, the Hessian is directly
proportional to the covariance matrix of the original Hamiltonian terms; related classical
learning problems are studied in, e.g., \cite{montanari2015, vuffray2016interaction}.
For noncommuting quantum Hamiltonians, the Hessian is no longer the ordinary covariance, and the
two difficulties in \cite{anshu2020sample} are reducing strong convexity to the variance of a
``reasonable'' operator, and relating this variance to the coefficients of the original Hamiltonian. The
authors address these issues by allowing \emph{quasi-local} operators, followed by a local twirl
which effectively restores locality. The effect of this twirl is analyzed using a result of
\cite{arad2016connecting} which controls the ``leakage'' caused by a local operator on eigenspaces
of a Hamiltonian. In our work, we make a simplification to this argument and adapt it to the
setting of SYK. We use the standard identity relating the Hessian to the
Bogoliubov--Kubo--Mori covariance \cite{petz1993bogoliubov} and compare it directly to the ordinary
variance, with a loss controlled by the spectral diameter. This simplifies several aspects of
\cite{anshu2020sample}; see \Cref{app:bounded_degree} for details. The remaining challenge is
adapting the ideas of \cite{arad2016connecting} to SYK. Their bounds depend on the sum of interaction
norms incident to a site, which is typically $\Theta(n^{3/2})$ for quartic SYK even after the
$\sigma_n$ normalization. Consequently, a direct application does not give the constant-temperature
control needed here. Instead, we relate the variance to the local-quench ratio,
\[
	R_{p,A}=\frac{Z_A(\beta,s,\vec g)}{Z(\beta,\vec g)},\qquad p=1+s/\beta\,.
\]
This is a Petz R\'enyi power \cite{petz1986quasi} between the Gibbs state and its conjugate by
$U_A=\Gamma_A$, and plays an analogous role to the energy-leakage bounds of
\cite{arad2016connecting}. Nested-commutator expansions already appear in that work; our analysis
averages over disorder before bounding the resulting terms. Counting the non-zero Gaussian
pairings and balancing this with the SYK normalization $\sigma_n$ bounds our thermal leakage
analogue. To pass from annealed to quenched estimates, we use an elementary, weaker version of the
commutation-index and Gaussian-concentration argument of \cite{anschuetz2025strongly}; their sharper
commutation-index estimates are unnecessary for our bounds.

Our quasi-polynomial time result structurally bears resemblance to the work of
\cite{haah2022optimal}. They begin with forming a series expansion of the log partition function (we
expand the bare partition function instead) and use the assumption of bounded interaction degree to
truncate the expansion at degree logarithmic in the inverse target accuracy (hence $O(\log n)$
for inverse-polynomial accuracy at fixed temperature). At this point,
the authors use Newton's method to solve a system of polynomial equations. Our approach differs in
several crucial ways. First, as mentioned in the introduction, the interaction degree of SYK is
$\Theta(n^3)$, counting quartic terms that overlap a given term, and a direct application of
\cite{haah2022optimal} would not cover constant inverse temperature. As such, after expanding the
series $Z(\beta, \vec g)$, we instead apply Wick--Isserlis \cite{isserlis1918formula} and carefully
count the resulting non-zero contributions, balancing this with the
contribution of $\sigma_n$ from the SYK normalization. Secondly, the result of
\cite{haah2022optimal} implies strong convexity at all points traversed by Newton's method.
Unfortunately, we are only able to show this result with high probability and it is not clear that
gradient descent would succeed in this setting. Rather, we instead appeal to the strong symmetry
exhibited by SYK and show that at Hermite degree $\leq 2$ in the disorder, we need to invert
a \emph{linear} $2\times 2$ system. This Hermite degree is distinct from the Taylor truncation
degree above. The remaining technical challenge is showing that higher Hermite degrees $d\geq3$
do not contribute much; proving this requires generalizing and expanding on the techniques of
\cite{zlokapa2026rigorous}.

More broadly, our partition-function analysis belongs to the zero-free and truncated-expansion
approach to quantum thermal algorithms developed in \cite{harrow2020classical}. For the
disorder-averaged estimates we use the Wick-pair polymer construction of
\cite{zlokapa2026rigorous} and the abstract polymer criterion of Koteck\'y and Preiss
\cite{kotecky1986cluster}, in the form given by \cite[Theorem~1]{ueltschi2004cluster}.

\paragraph{Barriers to time efficiency.} We briefly remark on a barrier to making our
sample-efficient algorithm time-efficient. Recent work of Zlokapa and Kiani~\cite{zlokapa2026syk} gives
a quasi-polynomial algorithm for thermal expectations under a zero-free-region assumption, supported
for SYK at all constant temperatures by large-$n$ arguments. Zlokapa~\cite{zlokapa2026rigorous}
rigorously establishes high-temperature SYK estimates, which we use in our analysis. This might suggest
running gradient descent over the space of disorder parameters and using such algorithms
to estimate the mismatch between the observables under a candidate set of parameters
versus under the true parameters. Unfortunately, it is unclear how to \emph{certify} that the
parameters encountered over the course of gradient descent correspond to Hamiltonians which are
``SYK''-like in the sense that these algorithms would succeed. This is reminiscent of the gap
between the complexity of finding ground states of the classical SK Hamiltonian versus
\emph{certifying} bounds on the ground state energy.
Indeed, Montanari~\cite{montanari2025optimization} showed that the former is achievable in
polynomial time, whereas Ghosh et al.~\cite{ghosh2020sum} gave evidence that certifying any bound
beyond the naive spectral bound is computationally hard by showing a degree-$n^\delta$
sum-of-squares lower bound. 

\paragraph{Concurrent work.} During the preparation of this manuscript, we were made aware of a recent work of Swingle~\cite{swingle2026single} which independently studied the relationship between local observables of the SYK model and the disorder parameters. While their work develops the connection using perturbative and heuristic arguments, our focus is on providing rigorous control of the contributions from higher-order terms in the expansion.

Throughout this work $n\geq 6$ is even, $\mc I_4=\binom{[n]}{4}$ is the set of $4$-tuples with elements in $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$,
$m=|\mc I_4|$, and
\[
    d_n=2^{n/2}
\]
is the dimension of the Hilbert space carrying the irreducible representation of the
$n$ Majorana operators.  We always use the normalized trace $\Tr(X)=d_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}_{\rm ordinary}(X)$, so that $\Tr(\Id)=1$. We define an instance of the SYK
model with disorder $\vec g$ as,
\[
  H_\mathrm{SYK}(\vec g)=H(\vec g) =\sigma_n\sum_{I\in\mc I_4}g_I\Gamma_I,\qquad \sigma_n =
  \sqrt{6/n^3}\,.
\]
Here, $\mc I_4 = \binom{[n]}4$ and $\Gamma_I$ are quartic Majorana terms, see \Cref{def:majorana}.

We use $\vec g=(g_I)_{I\in\mc I_4}$ for a fixed disorder vector and boldface for random
disorder: $\vec \bsg=(\bsg_I)_{I\in\mc I_4}$. Thus a disorder expectation is written
$\E_{\vec \bsg}f(\vec \bsg)$, where each coordinate $\bsg_I$ is drawn
independently from $\mc N(0,1)$. The scalar $\mu_\beta=\Tr[\rho_\beta H]$ is the mean energy; the vector
$\vec\mu_\beta=(\Tr[\rho_\beta\Gamma_I])_I$ consists of quartic expectations.
Define
\[
  Z(\beta,\vec g)=\Tr[e^{-\beta H(\vec g)}],\qquad
  \rho_\beta(\vec g)=\frac{e^{-\beta H(\vec g)}}{Z(\beta,\vec g)}.
\]
We write the log-partition function as $\Phi(\vec g) = \log Z(\beta, \vec g)$ when $\beta$ is fixed, and $F_{\vec g}(\beta) = \log Z(\beta, \vec g)$ when we are treating $\beta$ as the variable.

We work with the normalized trace so that $Z(0,\vec g)=1$ and $F_{\vec g}(0) = \log Z(0, \vec g) = 0$.
Because we use the normalized trace, $\rho_\beta$ satisfies
$\Tr(\rho_\beta)=1$, but its ordinary matrix trace is $d_n$.
The corresponding physical density matrix is therefore $\rho_\beta/d_n$. We write $Z_\mathrm{ann}(\beta)=\E_{\vec \bsg}Z(\beta,\vec \bsg)$ for the annealed
partition function. The subscript $\mathrm{meas}$ denotes measured moments or
the parameters recovered from them, for example $\vec g_\mathrm{meas}=(g_{\mathrm{meas},I})_{I\in\mc
I_4}$ and $\vec\mu_{\beta,\mathrm{meas}}=(\mu_{\beta,\mathrm{meas},I})_{I\in\mc I_4}$.

\begin{definition}[Multivariate Hermite polynomials]
	Multivariate Hermite polynomials are given by a multi-index $\vec d \in \N_0^m$, where the total degree is $|\vec d| =
	\sum_i d_i$. We use the normalized probabilists' polynomials
$\mathsf{Herm}_k=\mathrm{He}_k/\sqrt{k!}$, so
$\mathsf{Herm}_0=1$, $\mathsf{Herm}_1(x)=x$, and
$\mathsf{Herm}_2(x)=(x^2-1)/\sqrt2$. The corresponding multivariate Hermite polynomial is,
	\[
		\mathsf{Herm}_{\vec d}(\vec g) = \prod_{I \in \mc I_4} \mathsf{Herm}_{d_I}(g_I)\,.
	\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Majorana fermions]
	\label{def:majorana}
  Let $\{\psi_i\}_{i\in[n]}$ be Hermitian operators on the full $d_n$-dimensional
  Clifford space, satisfying $\{\psi_i,\psi_j\}=2\delta_{ij}\Id$. For
  $A=\{a_1<\cdots<a_k\}\subseteq[n]$, write
  \[
    \Gamma_A=\psi_{a_1}\cdots\psi_{a_k},\qquad \Gamma_\varnothing=\Id.
  \]
  These operators are unitary and
  $\Gamma_A^\dagger=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}\Gamma_A$. In particular, a quartic term
  $\Gamma_I$, $I\in\mc I_4=\binom{[n]}4$, is Hermitian, squares to the identity,
  and satisfies $\Tr[\Gamma_I\Gamma_J]=\1_{I=J}$ and $\Tr[\Gamma_I]=0$.
  Conjugations by a general $\Gamma_A$ always include the adjoint.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Gaussian norm]
	\label{def:gaussian_norm}
	Let $\vec{F}:\R^{d_1}\to\C^{d_2}$. We define the Gaussian norm,
	\[
		\|\vec{F}\|_{L^p} = \Paren{\E_{\vec \bsg \sim \mc N(\vec 0, \Id_{d_1 \times d_1})}
		\|\vec{F}(\vec \bsg)\|_2^p}^{1/p}\,.
	\]
	where $\|\vec{F}(\vec \bsg)\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm on $\C^{d_2}$.
\end{definition}

For scalar functions (and scalar--vector multiplication), this norm satisfies
H\"older's inequality: for $p,r,s\geq1$ with $\tfrac 1 p = \tfrac 1 r + \tfrac 1 s$,
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:holder}
	\|FG\|_{L^p} \leq \|F\|_{L^r} \|G\|_{L^s}\,.
\end{equation}

Additionally, we'll need a weighted Gaussian norm, which penalizes higher-degree terms.

\begin{definition}[Weighted Gaussian norm]
	\label{def:weighted_norm}
	For a function $\vec{F}(\vec g)$ with Hermite expansion $\sum_{d \geq 0} \Pi_d \vec{F}$,
	we write,
	\[
		\|\vec{F}\|_{2,s} = \sqrt{\sum_{d \geq 0} |s|^{2d} \|\Pi_d \vec{F}\|^2_{L^2}}\,.
	\]
	The value may be $+\infty$. Note by orthonormality of Hermite polynomials, $\|\vec{F}\|_{2,1} = \|\vec{F}\|_{L^2}$. 
\end{definition}
\noindent This norm can be related to the Gaussian norm via the following lemma. The proof is via
hypercontractivity.
\begin{lemma}
	\label{lem:norm_conversion}
	Let $\vec{F} : \R^{d_1}\rightarrow\C^{d_2}$ have finite weighted norm, let $p\geq2$, and set $s=\sqrt{p-1}$. Then,
	\[
		\|\vec{F}\|_{L^p} \leq \|\vec{F}\|_{2, s}\,.
	\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a scalar function, this is Gaussian hypercontractivity, applied to the
Ornstein--Uhlenbeck operator. For a vector-valued function, Minkowski's inequality in
$L^{p/2}$ gives $\|\vec{F}\|_{L^p}^2\leq\sum_j\|F_j\|_{L^p}^2$.
Apply the scalar bound to each real and imaginary component and sum.
\end{proof}

title: Exponential quantum advantages for decoded quantum interferometry in the streaming setting
abstract: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is a polynomial-time quantum algorithm introduced by Jordan et al. (Nature 2025). For a natural optimization problem, known as optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), it achieves approximation guarantees in regimes where all known classical algorithms require exponential time. Besides time, space is another central resource: storing and manipulating a massive input can be very challenging, especially when logical qubits carry substantial fault-tolerant implementation overhead. This motivates the following question: does DQI yield quantum advantages in memory, and can we prove it unconditionally? We give an affirmative answer to this question in the streaming setting. In particular, we consider a natural generalization of OPI using Hermite interpolation and Hasse derivatives, which asks for a low-degree polynomial satisfying as many constraints on its values and derivatives as possible. As a concrete example, we show [Quantum efficiency.] An adaptation of the DQI algorithm produces a polynomial satisfying $93\%$ of the constraints; moreover, it only reads the input stream in one pass, uses polylogarithmic space, and has polylogarithmic computation time per stream entry. [Classical hardness.] Any classical algorithm that produces an answer satisfying just $76\%$ of the constraints requires polynomial space, even if it can read the input stream with polynomially many passes and can use unlimited time. Our result provides a complete tradeoff curve for the tunable parameters, and implies that DQI has provable quantum advantages for the original OPI problem.
summary:
**TL;DR** The paper shows that decoded quantum interferometry (DQI), adapted to the one-pass streaming model, gives *unconditional* quantum memory advantages for a natural polynomial-fitting optimization problem. For a Hermite/multiplicity-code generalization of optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), a one-pass quantum streamer with polylog space and polylog per-entry time outputs a polynomial satisfying ~93.3% of the optimum, while any classical algorithm achieving even 75.001% needs polynomial space even with polynomially many passes and unlimited time. A matching classical upper bound completes the full approximation–space tradeoff curve.

**The big picture** Quantum algorithms for optimization usually claim speedups that are only conjectural, because nobody can rule out a clever classical algorithm. Here the authors switch the resource of interest from time to memory and passes over the data, where unconditional lower bounds are provable. They show that a recently proposed quantum optimization algorithm, when run on data arriving as a stream, finds good solutions using exponentially less memory than any classical method, no matter how much computation time it is given or how many times it rereads the input. Since memory is the scarcest resource in fault-tolerant machines, this is a concrete, verifiable form of quantum advantage for a natural optimization problem.

**Key contributions**
- Hermite OPI (HOPI): generalizes OPI from Reed–Solomon to univariate multiplicity codes, prescribing length-ℓ jets (Hasse derivatives) rather than single values.
- One-pass quantum streaming DQI: O(qℓ log q) space, poly(q,ℓ) time, achieving any α < α⋆ = (2+√3)/4 ≈ 0.93301.
- A near-optimal variant reaching any α < 1 with the same space and poly update time, but exponential postprocessing.
- Classical lower bound: any P-pass algorithm with α > 3/4 needs space ≳ q^{1+ℓ·κ(α)}/P, κ(α) = (4α−3)/(4α−2) — and a nearly matching one-pass classical upper bound, plus an O(qℓ log q)-space classical algorithm for α ≤ 3/4.
- A new list-recovery bound for multiplicity codes via hidden-derivative interpolation plus Kopparty's differential-root bound.

**How it works** The quantum side prepares, in one pass, the product state ⊗ᵢ(√(1−λ)|0⟩+√λ|ĥᵢ⟩), where phases encode membership bits; entries (i,z,𝟙[z∈Sᵢ]) only flip phases, so no input storage is needed. Projecting onto errors of weight ≤ d ≈ n/4, computing the syndrome, uncomputing the error via efficient unique decoding, and inverse Fourier transforming yields amplitudes ∝ P(score(u)), so measurement samples a polynomial with score concentrated at ½+√(λ(1−λ)); λ→¼ gives α⋆. For α→1 (λ→½) unique decoding fails, so the syndrome is augmented with the error on a random r = o(n) subset; a 2^{o(n)} list bound makes the augmented syndrome uniquely identifying, with exhaustive (space-cheap) decoding and a loss of ≤ r constraints. The classical bound goes through k = Θ(log q)-party communication with gadgetless lifting / structure-vs-randomness: list recovery caps the number of "dangerous" codewords exposed within a codimension budget T, while each newly dangerous codeword still has ~(1−1/k−ζ)n unexposed, pseudorandom queried bits, making it a solution with probability 2^{−Ω(n/log²n)}.

**Why it matters** This is a rare unconditional separation for a natural optimization problem, and the first where a *one-pass* quantum algorithm beats *many-pass* classical ones — unlike prior Max-DiCut/Max-2SAT streaming advantages, which constant-pass classical algorithms matched. The table of code families (Reed–Solomon, multiplicity, folded RS, LDPC, …) suggests a coding-theoretic taxonomy of Regev-reduction advantages.

**Caveats** The separation is for streaming space/passes, not time: the original OPI time advantage remains heuristic. Exponential space advantage requires ℓ growing polynomially in q, where the time advantage degrades to quasipolynomial. Lower bounds hold for random instances in a fixed grouped stream order. The near-optimal regime needs exponential postprocessing; whether polynomial-time postprocessing suffices is open, as is matching the 1/P pass dependence classically.
